such an exercise. Furthermore, the Committee desires that those 
States/UTs who have not made proposals for infrastructural 
development of the subordinate Courts in their state/UT, such as, 
Bihar, Punjab, Daman & Diu and Lakshadweep may be pursued and

Action Taken Reply 
2.1. Based on the requirement of infrastructure needs proj ected by the

2.1.1.  Funds are released to State Governments/ UTs as per following 
criteria.  
a) Requirement of funds projected by the respective High 
Courts for 2010-11 
b) Requirement of fund for the current year and 
c) Utilization of funds previously given to States/UTs 
2.1.2.  The matter of deve lopment of infrastructure of the subordinate 
courts is being regularly reviewed in the Supreme Court in the 
Interlocutory Application No.279/2010 in Writ Petition (C) 
No.1022/1989 in All India Judges „Association & Ors. Vs. Union of India 
& Ors. A monitoring mechanism has already been set up by formation of 
monitoring committees at Central, State and District level. 
2.1.3.  Funds to the tune of Rs. 38.17 crore have already been released to 
the State of Punjab during the current financial year. The proposal for 
release of funds to the State of Bihar is under process. The infrastructure 
required for subordinate judiciary in UTs is also being met by central 
government. 
Committee’s further observation 
2.2. The Committee notes the reply. However, the Committee de sires 
the Department to supply in detail  the nature of assistance provided by 
the Central Government to meet the infrastructure needs for the 
judiciary.  
Recommendation/observation 
3. The Committee is given to understand through the Outcome 
Budget (2012-13) of the Ministry that no timeline has been fixed for 
the implementation of this Scheme. It is, however, of the view that it 
is pertinent to impose timeline in the Action Plan on certain aspects 
of the Scheme, such as, setting up of Project Management Uni ts, 
consultation with stakeholders or proposed studies on the various 
aspects of the judicial reforms. The Committee feels that the 
experience with many Schemes launched by the Government face set-
backs after its implementation for two or three years due t o absence

Nyayalayas and the projects under the Centrally  Sponsored Scheme. 
Therefore, the Committee recommends that clear targets and 
timelines may be drawn and very close monitoring and regular 
appraisal should be made to ensure the successful implementation of 
the Scheme.  (Para 6.25, Ibid)  
Action Taken Reply 
3.1. Timelines for implementation of various strategic initiatives of 
National Mission have been drawn and approved by the Advisory 
Council of the National Mission in its meeting held on 15 -5-2012. The 
progress of the same would be monitored by the Advisory Council during 
its periodic meetings.  
3.1.1.  In order to overcome the problem faced in respect of Gram 
Nyayalayas scheme, a proposal for making Gram Nyayalayas Scheme a 
sub-component of the infrastructure development scheme of Subordinate 
judiciary has been prepared & forwarded to Department of Expenditure 
and Planning Commission for comments/views before obtaining the

3.1.2.  With the revised sharing pattern and higher budgetary allocations, 
utilization of funds u nder Centrally Sponsored Scheme of infrastructure 
development for subordinate judiciary has considerably improved.  
Committee’s further observation 
3.2. The Committee takes note of the work of the Department of 
Justice. However, the Committee desires to kn ow the parameters and 
evaluation methodology employed to measure the level of improvement. 
The Committee also desires to have the progress made so far in the 
Gram Nyayalaya Scheme proposed by the Department and also updates 
on the progress of the strategies taken up by the Advisory Council. 
EXTERNALLY AIDED PROJECT:  ACCESS TO JUSTICE FOR 
THE MARGINALIZED IN INDIA 
Recommendation/observation 
4. The Committee appreciates the approach of the A2J Project 
which has focused in empowerment of people through traini ng para 

 
legal workers of the community and creating the much needed 
linkage between Legal Services Authorities and Civil Society 
Organisations. The Committee, is however, constrained to point out 
that throughout the five years of the 11th Five Year Plan, t he 
Ministry has not been able to exhaust the allocations earmarked each 
year for the project. This is indication that the Government has a lot 
of scope for implementation of the project still left and therefore, 
should take concerted efforts in expanding i ts area and scope of 
operation when initiating the proposed new phase of the scheme to 
commence from 2013. The Committee desires that the details of the 
on-going project as well as plan of action for the proposed new phase 
of the project may be furnished to it at the time of furnishing ATRs. 
  (Para 6.39, ibid) 
Action Taken Reply 
4.1. Although the UNDP supported project on Access to Justice for 
marginalized people was slated to start in October 2008, it actually 
commenced in May 2009. It also took a longtim e to get other 
stakeholders, especially the Legal Services Authorities and the Judicial 
Academies on board. Moreover, the UNDP reduced its funding from US 
$ 5 million to US $ 3.8 million in 2010. Hence the project could not 
exhaust allocations earmarked for each year of the 11th Plan.  
4.1.1. Nevertheless, the Project has been successful in building synergies 
with National and State Legal Services Authorities, judicial academies, 
other Ministries including HRD, MHA, and WCD to avoid duplication 
and maximize efforts. The result is that a first -ever assessment of Legal 
Services Authorities has been done, legal literacy modules have been 
integrated in National Literacy Mission‟s adult literacy programme 
(Sakshar Bharat), adolescent girls under the SABLA scheme of WCD 
have been trained as paralegals and training modules have been prepared 
for judges‟ training.  
4.1.2.  In so far as legal empowerment of the people is concerned, the 
project has reached out to 20,00,000 people through a range of innovative 
strategies and materials on laws related to women‟s rights, tribal 
communities and the poor. Over 7,000 legal aid lawyers, paralegals, 
elected women representatives and representatives from various non -
government organizations and self-help groups have been trained to assist 
marginalized people access justice. 
4.1.3. This phase of the Project would end in December 2012. US $ 1.2 
million has been allocated for this year‟s activities, of which US $ 
748,077 was meant for supporting on -going project activities and US $ 

 
451,923 to be utilized to plan new activities. Some of the planned 
activities this year include training 60 lawyers in the 3 States of 
Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh as local skill pool to assist 
marginalized communities; creating a judges‟ training mo dule on anti -
trafficking; digitizing simplified legal information that can be uploaded 
on voice based kiosks to enhance legal awareness of marginalized 
communities; creating a legal awareness film; and supporting action 
research. 
4.1.4.  The details for th e project for the period 2013 -17 are under 
finalization. The final approval should be available by early 2013 for the 
full Project. 
4.1.5.  In addition to this Project, the Government has decided on its own 
to undertake a similar project in the eight North  Eastern States (including 
Sikkim) and in Jammu & Kashmir. The proposed “Access to Justice –NE 
and J&K” (A2J -NEJK) project seeks to address the needs of ordinary 
people, particularly, those who are poor and vulnerable and who are not 
strong enough to ensure that their rights are guaranteed. It would support 
justice delivery systems in improving their capacities to serve the people 
and in empower the ordinary people to demand improved services and 
access to their rights and entitlements. 
4.1.6. The A2J -NEJK project will be implemented between 2012 and 
2017, i.e. during the Twelfth Five Year Plan period. Total of Rs. 30 
crores have been earmarked for the Project for five years. The proposed 
project would seek to replicate – with necessary adaptation, activitie s 
presumed under the previous A2J project through in a different context. 
Beginning with a needs assessment study, the A2J -NEJK project will 
focus on legal empowerment of the people and seek to build convergence 
with existing activities of Legal Services A uthorities, Government 
Departments and Commissions. However, some new elements such as 
community policing, assisting under-trial prisoners and strengthening law 
school based legal aid clinics, are being concerned and would be 
introduced. The project has be en approved by the SFC and process to 
appoint consultants has been initiated. 
Committee’s further observation 
4.2. As The A2J project is mainly intended for the marginalized 
sections, the Committee desires to know the sections  that  are benefitted 
from the project annually,  the detail of mechanism through which  it 

 
reaches  to beneficiaries, the impact of project on beneficiaries, section-
wise, year wise,  state wise,  major issues and problems faced by the 
Department as well as the States in their implem entation of the project. 
The Committee also also desires to have  an action plan for 2013 -14 
and also for the remaining years of 12th plan. 
Recommendation/observation  
5. The Committee appreciates the ingenious scheme of e -Courts 
and is optimistic that it will help in more efficient management of 
subordinate courts, reduction in pending cases and increasing the 
speed of justice delivery processes. The Committee is however, 
constrained to point out that the expenditure of the Ministry in 2008 -
09 and 2011 -12 were way below the allocation projected. It is of the 
view that under utilization of funds are indicative of not achieving 
targets. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry 
should fix timelines and targets for the States while releasing the 
funds which would also play parameter for assessing their progress 
in implementation of the scheme.  (Para 6.45, ibid) 
Action Taken Reply 
5.1. Under the e -Courts Mission More Project (MMP), 14,249 district 
& subordinate courts are to be computerised by Marc h 2014. To initiate 
the computerisation of any district & subordinate court under the project, 
the readiness of the site at the court by way of preparation of a „Judicial 
Service Centre‟ (JSC) and a „Computer Server Room‟ (CSR) at a Court 
Complex along with the necessary civil and electrical works in the court 
rooms, is undertaken by the respective High Court for all the Courts 
under its jurisdiction. NIC provides the funds to the High Courts for site -
readiness on demand. Thereafter, the High Court engages a site 
preparation agency for getting the sites prepared thereafter. In majority of 
the States, the agency is the State PWD. Once the site is ready, the High 
Court intimates it to NIC. 
5.1.1. After receiving site readiness confirmation report from the High  
Court, NIC issues purchase orders for delivery and installation of the ICT 
equipments to its centrally empanelled vendors. The funds are disbursed 
to vendors in three stages: after delivery, after installation & after the 
work completion sign-off has been provided by the High Court.  

 
Under Utilisation of funds in 2011-12: 
5.1.2. The funds are earmarked for various project components such as 
creation of computer room, ICT training for judges and court staff, 
computer hardware, LAN, WAN connectivity, power b ackup, video 
conferencing, development of application software, data entry etc. The 
status of eCourt project in respect of each of these components is given in 
Annexure - III. 
5.1.3. The under-utilisation of funds in the last financial year has been on 
account of several difficulties faced in the implementation of the project. 
Out of 12,000 courts to be computerised by March 2012, a total of 9,634 
courts could be computerised. This is primarily because of the non 
availability of vendors for almost 6 months,  as well as, the delays by the 
vendors in meeting timelines committed by them. Moreover, finding 
suitable vendor who can ensure implementation at the taluka level, has 
been a challenge. The delay in site readiness thus continues to be a 
bottleneck. 
Timelines and targets for future: 
5.1.4. As on 31st December 2012, 11,810 courts have been computerised. 
The remaining 2,439 courts would be required to be computerised by 
March 2014. NIC has targeted to complete hardware installation in 
12,908 Courts by March 2013.  
5.1.5. To achieve the computerisation target within this financial year, 
DoJ has initiated monthly target setting and periodic reviews with the 
High Courts‟ Central Project Coordinators (CPC), state vendors and NIC, 
to monitor the Progress. These monthly targets are fixed on assessing the 
status of site readiness and the purchase orders issued for Hardware & 
Local Area Network (LAN) installation in consultation with NIC, 
Vendors and the Central Project Coordinators of the High Courts. Due to 
this there has been an improvement in the pace of implementation of the 
project and utilisation of funds. The month wise targets till March, 2013 
are given in a statement at Annexure - IV. 
5.1.6. In addition, a „Conference of all High Courts CPCs and NIC Co -
ordinators‟ is held periodically for review of project progress and resolve 
issues holding back the project completion . High Courts have been 
requested to have weekly follow -ups with the vendors to resolve issues 
and expedite the computerisation so that the targe ts set are achieved in a 
time bound manner.  
5.1.7. The eCommittee of the Supreme Court also convenes meetings of 
the Chairpersons of the Computer Committee of the High Courts for 

 
apprising them on the progress of the Project and discussing bottlenecks 
in implementation in each High Court.  
Committee’s further observation 
5.2. The under utilisation of funds is a serious issue and the 
Committee desires that in future the Department would  sort -out the 
issue as soon as possible. The Committee also desires to know the status 
of e -Courts established and the major challenges faced by the 
Department in running the e-Courts.  
Recommendation/observation 
6. It has also been observed that the BE (2012 -13) of Rs. 233.66 
crore has been pegged which is near two times hig her than the 
amount of RE (2011 -12) of Rs. 115 Crore. Mention may be made 
here that only roughly two -third of the RE (2011 -12) has been 
utilized. In that backdrop, the Committee is apprehensive as to 
whether the Department has the capacity to utilize the a llocation of 
Rs. 233.66 crore in 2012 -13. It, therefore, recommends that a clear 
timeline and target may be fixed and the progress of implementation 
should closely monitored so as to avoid time and cost overrun.             
   (Para 6.46, ibid)  
Action Taken Reply 
6.1. As already stated in response to recommendation number 6.45 
above, monthly targets have been fixed for each High Court till March 
2013 and a roadmap has been prepared for completion of the project by 
March 2014.  
6.1.1. Out of the allocated Rs. 233.66 Cr for the FY 2012-13, only Rs. 89. 
38 Cr has been allocated in the R.E. stage of the Project after a thorough 
exercise of fixing realistic targets for implementation of State I of the 
Project. Of the budgeted Rs. 233.66 Cr, Rs. 75 Cr had been earmarked for 
Stage-II of the project. For finalising the Stage-II of Project, consultations 
are being done with eCommittee, NIC and other stakeholders on the areas

has been commensurately reduced. 

 
6.1.2. Various additional measures are being taken up to monitor the 
implementation of the Project by various stakeholders to avoid time and 
cost overruns. Empowered Comm ittee, chaired by Secretary (Justice) 
which has representation from DeitY, Planning Commission, Department 
of Expenditure, Finance Ministry and NIC, gives strategic direction to the 
project as and when needed. Monthly review meetings are convened to 
monitor the Progress of the project. Weekly meetings are convened by 
NIC with the Vendors. eCommittee of Supreme Court holds meetings of 
Chairpersons of Computer Committees of the High Courts to discuss 
bottlenecks and to address them.  
6.1.3. In view of the abo ve, actions suggested by the Department related 
Parliament Standing Committee for completing the Project by March 
2014 are being taken. 
Committee’s further observation 
6.2. The Committee reiterates its views and desires the Department to 
supply information  on various additional measures taken to monitor 
the implementation of the project to avoid time and cost overruns.

CHAPTER-I
BRIEF OVERVIEW OF THE MINISTRY
1.0 The Union Ministry of Law and Justice comprises of three Departments, namely, the Department
of Legal Affairs, Legislative Department and Department of Justice and through the said Departments,
the Ministry assists in the process of orderly change directed towards realization of the objectives set
out in the Constitution.
DEPARTMENT OF LEGAL AFFAIRS
1.1 As per the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, the Department of Legal
Affairs renders advice to various Ministries/Departments of the Government of India on legal matters
and carry out the litigation work in various Courts, including the Supreme Court. Besides this, it is
also concerned with the appointment of Law Officers, namely the Attorney General of India, the
Solicitor General of India and the Additional Solicitor Generals of India, assists in entering into treaties
with foreign countries in matters of civil law inclusive of Hague Convention matters, executing
contracts and assurances of property on behalf of the President of India. It is also the nodal authority
in respect of Appellate Tribunal for Foreign Exchange, the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal and National
Tax Tribunal.
1.2 The Department of Legal Affairs has a two tier set up, namely, the Main Secretariat, New
Delhi and the Branch Secretariats at Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai and Bangalore. The nature of duties
discharged by the Main Secretariat and Branch Secretariats can be broadly classified into two areas–
Advice work and Litigation work. Advice caters to Central Government Departments/Offices at Centre
and in States/UTs and Litigation work relates to Central Administration Tribunal (CAT), High Courts
and Supreme Court.
1.3 The following are the organisations/institutions, which come under the overall supervision of
Department of Legal Affairs and get Grant-in-aid for their research works:–
(a) National Legal Services Authority (NALSA):- The National Legal Services Authority
has been constituted under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 to monitor and
evaluate implementation of legal aid programmes and to lay down policies and principles
for making legal services available under the Act. The NALSA issues guidelines for the
State Legal Services Authorities to implement the legal aid programmes which are in turn
discharged through the following services:–
(i) Free Legal Services:-  It includes court fees, process fee and all charges payable
or incurred in connection with any legal proceedings, providing Advocate in legal
proceedings, etc.
(ii) Lok Adalats:- Lok Adalat is a forum where the disputes/cases pending in the
court of law or at pre-litigation stage are settled/compromised amicably. The
Lok Adalat has been given statutory status under the Legal Services Authorities
Act, 1987.
(b) Law Commission of India:-  The Law Commission of India is a non-statutory body,
constituted by the Government once in three years. The Commission was first constituted

2
in 1955. It consists of a Chairman, three full-time Members, one Member-Secretary and
three or more part-time Members, depending upon the nature of work. Law Commission
Reports are considered to be primary source of law reforms for Parliament, as well as
the judiciary.
(c) Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT):- Section 252 of the Income Tax Act, 1961
provides that the Central Government shall constitute an Appellate Tribunal consisting of
as many Judicial Members and Accountant Members as it thinks fit, to exercise the
powers and discharge the functions conferred on the Appellate Tribunal by said Act.
(d) Appellate Tribunal of Foreign Exchange (ATFE):- The Appellate Tribunal of Foreign
Exchange was established on 1
st June 2000 vide Government of India Notification No.
S.O. 531 (E), dated 1.6.2000 issued under section 18 of the Foreign Exchange Management
Act, 1999 (FEMA),
(e) Indian Law Institute (ILI):- The Indian Law Institute registered under the Societies
Registration Act, 1860 is engaged in research in the field of law.
(f) International Centre for Alternate Dispute Resolution (ICADR):- The International
Centre for Alternate Dispute Resolution was registered under the Societies Registration
Act, 1860 on 31
st May 1995. It is an autonomous organisation working under the aegis
of the Ministry of Law and Justice (Department of Legal Affairs).
(g) Bar Council of India (BCI):- The Bar Council of India is a statutory body constituted
under the Advocates Act 1961, which has been empowered among other things to lay
down standards of professional conduct and etiquette for lawyers, maintain and improve
the standard of legal education in the country.
(h) Institute of Constitutional and Parliamentary Studies (ICPS):- The Institute of
Constitutional and Parliamentary Studies is a private body engaged in research in the field
of Constitutional and Parliamentary Studies and came into existence in 1965.
LEGISLATIVE DEPARTMENT
1.4 The Legislative Department acts mainly as a service provider in so far as the legislative
business of the Union Government is concerned. The Department is entrusted with legislative matters
and is responsible for drafting of all Government Bills and Ordinances and scrutiny and vetting of
subordinate legislations sponsored by various Union Ministries/ Departments. Rendering assistance to
Parliament and Joint/Standing Committees in respect to Bills before its enactment. It is also administratively
concerned with certain matters such as the Code of Civil Procedure, Limitation and Arbitration,
Contracts, Personal Laws, Evidence and Transfer of Property as regards legislation. There are over
hundred Central Acts falling under these subjects.
1.5 The Department has two wings under it mainly:-
(i) Institute of Legislative Drafting and Research : With a view to increase the availability
of trained legislative draftsmen in the country, the Institute of Legislative Drafting and
Research was established as a Wing of the Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and
Justice in January, 1989.
(ii) Of ficial Languages Wing and Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan : The Official Languages Wing
is a successor Organisation of the Official Languages (Legislative) Commission under the
Legislative Department. It has been entrusted with the preparation and publication of a
standard legal terminology for use in all Official Languages; authoritative texts in Hindi of
all Central Acts and Ordinances and Regulations promulgated by the President, all rules,

3
regulations and orders made by the Central Government under any Central Act and
authoritative texts of all Central Acts and Ordinances and Regulations promulgated by the
President in the respective Official Languages of the States and to arrange for the
translation of all Acts passed and Ordinances promulgated in any State into Hindi, if the
texts of such Acts or Ordinances are in a language other than Hindi.
1.6 Election Commission of India:  Legislative Department is also administratively concerned with
the Election Commission of India and Election laws connected with election to Parliament and State
Legislatures and to the offices of the President and the Vice-President. There is a separate Demand
No.63 for the Election Commission of India.
DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE
1.7 The duties of the Department of Justice, as per the Government of India (Allocation of
Business) Rules, 1961, include the administration of justice and the processing of appointment of
judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, appointment of Judicial Commissioners and Judicial
Officers in Union Territories, creation of All India Judicial Service and extension/exclusion of the
Jurisdiction of a High Court to a Union Territory.
1.8 The following institutions/autonomous bodies/policy initiatives come directly under the overall
supervision of Department of Justice:
(a) Supreme Court of India:- There is a separate demand No.65 (Appropriation) pertaining
to the Supreme Court of India. The expenditure to be incurred on the Supreme Court of
India is ‘Charged’  expenditure.
(b) Family Courts/Special Courts:-  The Family Court Act, 1984 was enacted with a view
to providing for establishment of Family Courts, to promote conciliation in and secure
speedy settlement of disputes relating to marriage, family affairs and related matters. In
accordance with the provisions of section 3 of the Act, the State/UT Governments can
establish Family Courts in the areas comprising districts, towns, city in the States having
population of ten lakhs. Even the States/UTs are competent to establish such court in
those areas with the State/UT having a population less than ten lakhs in consultation with
the concerned High Court.
(c) National Judicial Academy:-  The National Judicial Academy was registered as a Society
under the Societies Registration Act and came into existence with effect from 17
th August,
1993. The affairs of the Academy are managed by a Governing Council, which is chaired
by the Chief Justice of India. The registered office of the Academy is in Supreme Court
Building at New Delhi and another office was established in August, 2000 at Bhopal. The
main objectives of the Academy are to impart training to the Judicial Officers of the
States/Union territories and to study the court management and administration of justice
in States and Union territories.
(d) Centrally Sponsored Scheme:- The government is implementing a Centrally Sponsored
Scheme (CSS) for development of infrastructure facilities for judiciary since 1993-94.
The scheme covers construction of court buildings and residential accommodation of
Judicial officers/judges covering only Subordinate courts. Under the Scheme, funds are
provided to the States to augment their capacities for infrastructure development of the
District and Subordinate Courts. The modified CSS is to be implemented in a Mission
Mode approach over the years 2011-16 under the National Mission.
(e) National Mission for Justice Delivery and Legal Reforms:  Set up for five years in
2011, and became fully functional with effect from the financial year 2012-13. The twin

4
goals of the Mission includes increasing access by reducing delays and arrears in the
system and enhancing accountability at all levels through structural changes and setting
performance standards and facilitating enhancement of capacities for achieving such
performance standards. The four schemes proposed to be pursued under the Mission are
as under;
(i) National Mission-Action Plan Implementation
(ii) Action Research and Judicial Reforms
(iii) Setting-up of Model Courts (Phase I)
(iv) Access to Justice- Government of India Project (New Scheme).
(f) Access to Justice- Externally Aided Project (UNDP assisted)
The Project started in 2009 with support under the United Nations Development Programme
(UNDP). The Project is being implemented in 7 States (Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand,
Madhya Pradesh, Orissa, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh) and aims to strengthen access to
justice for the marginalized - particularly women, scheduled castes, scheduled tribes and
minorities - by supporting strategies and initiatives that seek to address the barriers they
face.
(g)  Computerization of District and Subordinate Courts
E-courts Mission Mode Project Phase-I & II :- This is a scheme proposed in the
12
th Plan with components such as computerisation of 1000 new Courts, use of solar
energy under e-Courts Project, computerisation of the Public Prosecutors Office,
videoconferencing facility for jails, enhancement of ICT infrastructure of courts, digitization
of old case records, computerisation of Judicial libraries, up-gradation of application
software, SMS based services, Touch Screen Kiosks with a provision of R1280 crore
which would be spread over a period of five years.
(h) Establishment of Gram Nyayalayas under the Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008:-  The
Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 has been enacted by the Parliament to provide for the
establishment of the Gram Nyayalayas at the grass root level for the purpose of providing
speedy and inexpensive access to justice to the citizens at their door steps. The Central
Government would meet 50% of the recurring expenses to be incurred on the setting up
of these courts in the first three years subject to a ceiling of  3.20 lakhs per annum.
(i) The  Thirteenth Finance Commission:-  With the objective of improving justice delivery,
Thirteenth Finance Commission (TFC) has recommended a grant of  5000 crore over its
award period of 2010-15. This grant is aimed at providing support to improving judicial
outcomes, and is allocated for initiatives such as - operation of morning/evening courts/
shift courts, Alternate Dispute Resolution (ADR) Centres, training of mediators/conciliators
for ADR Centres, holding of Lok Adalats, provision of Legal Aid, training of judicial
officers, assistance to State Judicial Academies, training of Public Prosecutors, appointment
of Court Managers, maintenance of Heritage Court Buildings, etc.

3.7 The Commission has further informed that it has also taken up countrywide Systematic V oters

12
maximize voter’s turnout in order to strengthen the Indian democracy. There is a scientific focus and

and others in the electoral process. This also entails the involvement of a large number of partner
agencies, media and educational institutions right up to the polling station level. Campaign for informed

3.8 The Committee appreciates the SVEEP programme under-taken by the Commission and

so as to make our democracy more vibrant. However, the Committee feels that the actual
target of voters awareness programme should be clearly defined so that the country’s valuable
resources do not go waste. It should accordingly, implement the programme in a pre-determined
phased manner beginning with States nearer to elections.
3.9 Another important area of concern is the use of EVMs in the elections. An elector has
every right to know whether the candidate whom he has cast his vote through the electronic
voting machine has actually gone for that candidate. This is not possible in the present system.
The Election Commission has reported that they are in the process of attaching printer to the
EVM on a limited scale to begin with  for giving a printed copy of the vote cast by the elector
at the polling station. The Committee appreciates the initiative taken by the Election Commission
of India to give a printed confirmation of the vote one has cast for the candidate of his/her
choice to confirm that no manipulation in the voting machine has occurred after the vote has
been cast by the elector. The Committee hopes that this measure of the Election Commission
would go a long way in establishing the faith of the electors in the EVMs and also the
processes in the conduct of the elections.

MODEL CODE OF CONDUCT
3.18 Model Code of Conduct is a set of guidelines laid down by the Election Commission to govern
the conduct of political parties and candidates in run-up to an election. It is intended to provide a level
playing field for all political parties, keep the campaign fair and healthy, avoid clashes and conflicts
between parties and ensure peace and order. Its main aim is to ensure that the ruling parties, either at
the Centre or in the States, do not misuse its official position to gain an unfair advantage in an election.
3.19 During the examination of the Demands for Grants (2012-13) of the Department, Members
were of the view that some paras of the Model Code of Conduct are already covered by other statutes
and the Election Commission still regards the Model Code of Conduct as voluntary in nature. The ECI,
in its Action Taken Replies on the Demands for Grants (2012-13) replied that.–
“….in the absence of any law or statute, the Election Commission uses its power conferred by
Article 324 of the Constitution and issues need based instructions/ directions regulating the
conduct of free and fair elections. This is necessitated because even after the lapse of 22 years
after the All-Party Committee on Electoral Reforms submitted its report, no statute covering
issues in respect of these reforms has been framed empowering the Commission to conduct free
and fair election. The Commission cannot avoid its responsibility by remaining a silent
spectator and merely paying lip service to the cause of electoral reforms and conduct of free
and fair elections in the country.”
3.20 The Committee had observed in its Report on the ATRs of the Government that.–
The Committee observes that Model Code of Conduct is a voluntary agreement between the
parties for regulating the conduct of political parties and its members, etc., during the process

14
of elections to Assemblies and Parliament. Its legal status is a grey area. After hearing the
views of the official of the Ministry of Law and considering the problems which have erupted
in the country, from time to time, in the last few years, the Committee feels that the Code,
which was voluntary in nature at one time has not remained so after insertion of para 16 A
in the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968, which authorizes the Election
Commission, to suspend or withdraw the recognition of political parties in case of violation
of Code of Conduct. Besides, some of the paras in the code attract penal provisions in other
laws.
3.21 The Committee notes the submissions of the Election Commission. It, however, reiterate
its earlier recommendation on the issue and accordingly, urges the Government and ECI to
review the Model Code of Conduct. In this context, the Committee recommends deletion of
para 16A of the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment ) Order, 1968, and incorporate
the same in the Representation of People Act, 1951. The Committee also takes up this
opportunity to observe that the Code of Conduct be made effective from the date of Press
Note/Press Conference declaring the elections. The Committee, in this context, recommends
that the Code of Conduct should be made effective from the date of notification of elections
and not from the date of the declarations of the elections.

3.31 During the course of discussion in the meeting some of the Members expressed that the
EVM’s are not trustworthy and tamperable. Members also expressed their reservation with regard to
the transparency in voting through the EVMs. Members stated that a voter has every right to have
confirmation that his vote has gone to the candidate for whom he had voted. However, in voting
through EVMs, an elector is not sure that his/her vote has gone to the candidate of his choice as he
does not receive any visual impression as on paper assuring him/her that his vote has been rightly cast.
3.32 The representative, Election Commission while deposing before the Committee during the
Demands for Grants (2013-14) explained that:
“…The Commission has taken this suggestion very seriously. And what you are talking about
is technically known as a Voter-verified Paper Audit Trail, so that you can connect your
printer to the EVM and when a person casts his vote, the printer prints the vote which can
be seen. It was also mentioned that if this vote is taken outside, then people can be intimidated
and influenced and so, he should not be allowed to take the vote outside; he should be able
to see it when it falls in a box and which can be counted later on. Sir, I am very happy to
report that last month, the design of the VVP AT system has been finalized by our Technical
Expert Committee. The design has been finalized. The Commission has already placed orders
for buying 150 printers from BEL and 150 printers from ECIS. We hope to get these printers
within a month or, maximum, in one-and-a-half to two months. We hope to use this VVP AT
system is some by-election very soon. We would like to first use it in some by-election and only
when we succeed would we like to increase its usage, but we are trying to do it.”
3.33 W ith the development of ICT, the question of e-voting has become important. Some Members
during the discussions on the Demands for Grants (200013-14) raised the question on the provision
of e-voting. On this, the representative of Commission replied that:–
“…we have had a lot of thinking on this subject. By ‘e-voting’, you probably mean voting
on the internet because if you mean to say electronic-voting, we already have Electronic Voting
Machines. But with regard to internet-based voting, currently, we feel that even with EVMs,
there have been so many allegations, so, at this stage, if we go to internet-based voting, it
will probably lead to too much of controversies. So, at this point of time, the Commission does
not feel to go in for the same.”

3.34 The Committee notes the view-point of the Election Commission that the issue of
e-voting need to be studied and researched in larger depth and it may not be introduced as
of now. As regards the use of EVMs, the Committee desires that records of cases of mal-
function and tempering of EVMs as pointed out by Members, if so occurred, may be kept so

3.35 During the course of the presentation before the Committee, some of the Members pointed
out that V oter Awareness Programme organised by some of NGOs in States are being held for

recommendations of this Committee, the Election Commission of India has sought R18.4 crores

their participation in the election process is voluntary, to the maximum, constructive and
in the right perspective. This will further deepen the roots of democratic set up in our
country which is our asset.

4.1 The main work of the Department is to render legal advice to the different Ministries and
Departments of the Central Government on legal matters including interpretation of the Constitution
and laws. The Department also is in charge of handling litigation work of the Central Government in

21
the Supreme Court, High Courts, District Courts, Tribunals, engagement of Counsels to appear on
behalf of the Union of India in different Courts and Tribunals.
4.2 The Secretary, Department of Legal Affairs during the Demands for Grants (2013-14) said that
they are:
…are simply representing them because the subject belongs to them. We are a service Department.
We are giving legal advice service to various Ministries and Departments. We represent various
Departments in Courts at their instance. We  do not formulate our own view.
4.3 Some key areas covered under the budgetary allocations of the Department of Legal Affairs
are enumerated in the succeeding paragraphs.
APPELLATE TRIBUNAL FOR FOREIGN EXCHANGE (ATFE)
4.4 Despite the vacant post of Chairperson for a long time the Budget allocation for ATFE was
raised in BE 2013-14 to R1.23 crore against the R1.03 crore in RE 2012-13.
4.5 Committee is seriously concerned about the pending vacancy of Chairperson, and feels
that it may severely affect the working of important body like the Appellate Tribunal for
Foreign Exchange (ATFE). The Committee urges the Ministry to immediately fill up the
existing vacancies in ATFE so that the work may not be compromised.
INCOME TAX APPELLATE TRIBUNAL (ITAT)
4.6 For the year 2013-14 a sum of R50.35 crores has been allocated/sanctioned for Income Tax
Appellate Tribunal under the Major Head ‘2020’ for meeting its administrative expenses against RE
(2012-13) of  R47.99 crore. The Actual Expenditure during 2011-12 was  R45.25 crore. R10.02 crore
has also been allocated under Capital Outlay on ‘Other Administrative Services’ under Major Head
‘4070’ in BE 2013-14, against R1.02 in RE 2012-13.
4.7 The Department informed the Committee that, under the head ‘Salary’ in respect of ITAT, an
amount of R35.00 crore was kept in BE 2012-13 which was enhanced to R36.45 crore at RE stage
against the demand of ITAT of R38.00 crore (approx) under this head. This was due to allocation
of lesser fund in RE 2012-13 by the Ministry of Finance under ‘Salary’ head ( R91.97 crore).
Thereafter, the ITAT requested to augment the fund under the ‘Salary’ head to R4.8 crore for the year
2012-13. In this regard, an amount of R1.81 crore was re-appropriated to the head ‘Salary’ in respect
of ITAT with the approval of the Ministry of Finance and the RE 2012-13 in respect of ITAT
was enhanced to R49.60 crore. From this, it may be seen that there is only a minor increase in
BE 2013-14 from RE 2012-13 in respect of ITAT i.e. R75.00 lakh. This is due to increase under
various heads i.e. Salary, Medical Treatment and D.T.E etc as per the demand received from ITAT.

to dispose of Single Member Cases (SMC) and Wealth Tax Cases (WTC) to reduce pendency of

4.10 The Annual Report (2012-13) further reflects that there are 63 sanctioned Benches of I.T.A.T.
wherein the required strength of the Members is 126 and presently have 87 Members and some of
the Benches are not regualarly functioning resulting in increase of pendency. Therefore, there is a need
to utilize information for dispensation of justice in the I.T.A.T by introducing E-Courts/E-Benches and
it will make non-functioning Benches operational to reduce pendency of these Benches. Accordingly,
Nagpur Bench has been connected to Mumbai Benches and started E-Court hearing of appeals by
video conferencing since December 10,2012
4.11 As regards the filling up of vacancies in the present sanctioned Benches of the ITAT is 63 and
the required strength of the Members is 126. However the present strength of Members is only 87.
During the Demands for Grants (2013-14) presentation, the Secretary, Department of Legal Affairs has
submitted that:–
…we had advertised 35 vacancies and we could get only 16 members. So, that is the backlog.
We are now in the process of advertising 48 vacancies.
4.12 The Committee expresses its concern over the mounting pendency in the Income Tax
Appellate Tribunal (ITAT). The inability for some Benches to function regularly due to
vacancies in the posts of Members is seen as totally undesirable by the Committee. Accordingly,
the Committee urges the Department and the ITAT to make timely and concerted efforts in
filling up the vacancies. The Committee feels that the filling–up of the vacancies, both in the
higher and lower grades along with the computerization of ITAT will go a long way in reducing
the pendency of cases. Thus, the Committee recommends that the vacant posts in ITAT be
filled within a period of three months.

Volunteers, which is being done by NALSA periodically, will give an insight into areas that call

OFFICIAL LANGUAGES WING

legislation in English, the Legislative Department is responsible for preparing and handling all principal
and subordinate legislations in Hindi language as well, which is the official language of the Union as
per Article 343 of the Constitution.
5.3 An amount of R7.98 crore has been allocated to the official language wing in 2013-14. There

Grants (2013-14) informed the Committee that, the funds allocated were not optimally utilized to the

VIDHI SAHITYA PRAKASHAN (VSP)
5.5 Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan brings out various publications of legal literature, including law books
and law journals, in Hindi containing Hindi translations of selected judgments of the Supreme Court
and High Courts on cases pertaining to constitutional, civil and criminal laws. It also holds exhibitions
in various States for giving wide publicity to legal literature available in Hindi and to promote their
sales.
5.6 In BE (2013-14) the allocation of R4.91 crore has been made to VSP against R4.30 crore in
RE (2012-13). The Committee has been informed that the VSP has constantly failed to utilize its earlier
grants. The Department informed the Committee that during the years 2009-10, 2010-11 and
2011-12 the whole amount allocated to VSP could not be utilized by it due to the same reasons as
stated in Para 5.4 above.
5.7 The Committee takes note of the activities being taken up by the Official Language
Wing (OLW). The Committee feels that the OLW should also get translated the Bills/Acts in
more regional languages so that these can be used at the lower/subordinate level courts, where
the litigation work in done in regional languages.
5.8 The Committee takes note of the increase in the overall Budgetary allocation to the
Legislative Department. The Committee appreciates the austerity measures undertaken by the
Department following the directives of the Finance Ministry. The Committee suggests that the
VSP should upgrade on the quality of its publications in terms of layout, content and context.
It should also explore scope of bringing out e-books and e-publications. In Committee’s view,
active engagement of States in the promotion and publicity of its literature available in Hindi
by holding frequent competitions, seminars and conferences for school/college going students,
through the respective States, may increase the distribution of its books and journals among
more people.
INSTITUTE OF LEGISLATURE DRAFTING AND RESEARCH
5.9 With a view to increasing the availability of trained legislative draftspersons in the country, the
Institute of Legislative Drafting and Research was established as a Wing of the Legislative Department,
Ministry of Law and Justice in January, 1989 to impart theoretical as well as practical training in
Legislative Drafting. Since its inception, Twenty four Basic Courses(3 months duration) and Fourteen
Appreciation Courses (15 days duration) have been conducted by the institute for imparting training

30
in drafting of legislation, principal as well as subordinate legislation, to middle level Law Officers of
the Central/State Governments/Union Territory Administrations. Besides, the institute has given on-the-
job practical training including lectures on legislative drafting and its techniques to a total of 406
trainees in the past from various foreign countries sponsored by the Bureau of Parliamentary Studies
and Training, Lok Sabha Secretariat.
5.10 The Committee was informed that during the last financial year, 1 Basic Course and 2
Appreciation Courses have been conducted, in which around 70 officers participated. Recently, the
Ministry of Law and Justice has approved in principle a Road Map for the Legislative Drafting
Institute, envisaging (a) conduct of courses in Legislative Drafting in Hindi (b) for giving training to
the officers of Legislative Department in International Institutes imparting training in legislative drafting
(c) developing the Institute of Legislative Drafting and Research as a institution of national importance
and (d) action for getting the LDI Section ISO certified.
5.11 The Secretary, Legislative Department while deposing before the Committee during the Demands
for Grants (2013-14) submitted that, presently they are functioning with limited numbers of drafting
personnel at various levels. The Secretary said that:
“… this is a very, very important Department, in the sense that all the legislations, all the
Bills which are introduced in the House are drafted by my officers. Unfortunately, the staff
strength, the officers who actually draft the Bills has remained stagnant for quite some time.
I have collected some figures and I feel that there is an urgent need, an inescapable need, for
augmenting the drafting personnel available in the Legislative Department at various levels.
At present, there are only 34 drafting personnel in the Legislative Department, which is not
commensurate with the workload currently being handled by this Department… I think there
is a need to increase this strength.”
5.12 The Committee appreciates the work undertaken by the Department during the last
financial year. The Committee also takes note of the shortage of drafting personnel at various
levels. The Committee takes serious note of the shortage of drafting personnel as submitted
to it and urges the Department to coordinate with the Institute of Legislature Drafting and
Research (ILDR) in this regard for creation of a strong pool of experts in legislative drafting
from where it can draw it’s requirement. It is also of the considered view that the quality of
drafting of legislations should not be compromised at any cost and therefore, such an
important Department should be allowed to increase its strength so that the quality of
legislations drafted may not be affected.
5.13 A good twenty four years has gone by since the establishment of the ILDR in January,
1989. In this context, the Committee is constraint to note that a mere 24 Basic Courses of
three months duration each and 14 Appreciation Courses of fifteen days duration each has
been conducted in these fourteen years. The Committee is of the opinion that the institute has
not performed to its optimum. In this context, the Committee wishes to refer to the oral
submission of Secretary, Legislative Department stating that there is urgent need for augmenting
the Department’s personnel for legislative drafting which reflects the urgency of requirement
of skilled manpower. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the ILDR should frame
target of conducting a minimum of two Basic Courses and two Appreciation Courses each
financial year in view of the importance and necessity of having a strong pool of experts in
legislative drafting.
5.14 The Committee has also been continuously reminding the Department to expedite the
process of acquiring of land and construction of building for ILDR. However, the Committee
is again disappointed to note that only a token amount of  1 lakh has been allocated to ILDR
in BE 2013-14. The Committee believes that an institution of such a stature needs to have its
own building to carry out its functions.

on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice on the Representation of the People (Amendment)

on the 20th August, 2010 and passed by both the Houses of Parliament which was enacted as the
Representation of the People (Amendment) Act, 2010 (36 of 2010).
5.16 The Committee was appraised that in pursuance of the provision of the above said Act, the
Registration of the Electors Rules, 1960 has been amended vide the Registration of Electors (Amendment)
Rules, 2011 which has been notified in the Gazette of India on the 2nd February, 2011. These Rules
were subsequently amended vide the Registration of Electors (Second Amendment) Rules, 2011 on
23rd February, 2011 so as to enable publication of the rolls on the website of the Chief Electoral
Officer of the concerned State as well as to submit the application for registration accompanied by
self-attested copies of passport, visa, etc., instead of getting it attested by the Indian Missions abroad.
5.17 The representative, ECI while deposing before the Committee during the Demands for Grants
(2013-14) submitted that:
“…the law was amended in 2011 and the voting rights were given to NRIs in 2011. After that,
the Commission amended the rules with the help of Law Ministry and a new form, Form 6A,
has been prescribed for the NRIs to actually apply to register themselves as voters. It is a fact
that not very large number of people have registered themselves as NRIs. I don’t have the exact
number, but it is only in few thousands that people have registered themselves as NRI voters.
We are, of course, trying a lot with the help of Ministry of Overseas Indian Affairs and with
the help of the Ministry of External Affairs to popularize registration of voters. We have given
these forms on our website and links have been provided on the website of the Ministry of
External Affairs also. We have also requested Ministries to publicize it in foreign newspapers
where a large number of Indian people are living. We have also made a provision that if NRIs
happen to come to India for a short period of time, they can submit their application here
itself and we will register them…”
5.18 The Committee appreciates the initiatives taken by the Department in facilitating the
voting right to Non-resident citizens of India and also the simplification of the process of
submission of application for registration. However, the Committee feels that these few
thousands registrations need to be increased to justify the voting rights that has been
conferred on the NRIs. The Committee recommends the Government to take more initiatives
in this regard.

6.7 Central financial assistance was started in 2002-03 for setting up of Family Courts in States.

6.11 Family Courts are an important instrument to reduce the pendency of cases. Under

set up a Family Court for every area in the State comprising a city or a town whose population
exceeds one million. In other areas of the States, the Family Courts may be set up if the State
Governments deem it necessary. However, the Committee is not satisfied with the slow pace
of establishment of Family Courts in different parts of the country even after two decades of
the enactment of the Family Court Act, 1984. The Committee is given to understand that lack
of finances is one of the main cause for slow pace of setting up of Family Courts. There is
perhaps a persistent demand from the States for higher assistance for setting up such Courts
both for meeting the expenditure for establishing such Courts and also for meeting the cost
for running them. The Committee impress upon the Ministry of Law & Justice to review the
funding pattern so that more Family Courts are set up.

6.30 The Committee is more than convinced that speedy and efficient dispensation of justice
is the need of the country today and for meeting this objective, the fast track Courts can play
a major constructive role. With the Central assistance of 75% (90% in case of North Eastern
States), the Committee does not foresee any hesitation on the part of the States to set up such
fast track Courts for speedy trial in serious crimes against society including those involving
children, the elderly or the vulnerable sections of the Society. The Committee is convinced that
in case we succeed in curtailing the trial period in the Courts, a definite message would go
in the Society creating a feeling in the mind of the common man to abide by the laws due
to the fear of being punished. Such a scenario in Committee’s view would help in bringing
down the rate of crime in the country. The Committee accordingly, recommends that the
Department of Justice should take all possible steps to ensure that the fast track Courts are
set up in appropriate situations in the States and the States do not face impediments in this
regard.
(i) National Mission-Action Plan Implementation:
6.31 The activities under the tentative Action Plan of the National Mission are explained in brief as
under:
(a) Policy and legislative changes such as All India Judicial Service, Litigation Policy, Judicial
Impact Assessment, Amendment in the N.I. Act and the Arbitration & Conciliation Act,
Legal Education Reforms, etc.
(b) Re-engineering procedures and Alternate Methods of Dispute Resolution such as identification
of bottlenecks, procedural changes in court processes, statutory amendments to reduce and
disincentives delays, Fast tracking of procedures, appointment of court managers, etc.
(c) Focus on Human Resource Development such as strengthening State Judicial Academies,
Training of Public Prosecutors and strengthening National Judicial Academy and Training
of mediators.
6.32 In order to carry-out above mentioned activities for implementation of the Action Plan of the
Mission, a provision of R5.00 crore has been kept under B.E. 2013-14 for effective implementation
of various initiatives to be undertaken under the National Mission.

6.33 The Committee takes notes of the serious activities envisaged under the tentative
Action Plan of the National Mission. In Committee’s view, the various actions enumerated in
the Action Plan are complimentary and supplementary to each other and would definitely prove
to be helpful in not only in speeding up the disposal of cases but also enhancing the quality
of their disposal. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should work on the Action
Plan in all seriousness and at the right earnest so that there is considerable progress of action
in the financial year ahead. The Committee however, reiterates its recommendations on the

“…in addition to the justifications already brought the Committee on earlier occasions, it may

or States where they located, the Supreme Courts of India represents National Symbol. It is the
single Court identified with the country. It is a unifying force where regionalism of other
divisive element has no role to play. Having a Permanent Bench of the Court in other part
could easily disturb this and lead to various divisive elements creeping into the system. It could
impair the unity and the integrity of the Court and undermine its importance.”
7.4 The Committee feels that the unwillingness towards establishment of the other Benches
of the Supreme Court cannot be justified on the grounds that it would attract a cumbersome
process of Constitutional amendment and endanger national unity. The reply that Supreme
Court represents national symbol and a unifying force remains intact even if the benches of
the Supreme Court are set up as there are High Courts which have jurisdiction over more
than one State. The Committee strongly feels that it does not play any divisive role in any
way. The Committee, therefore reiterates its earlier view for establishment of other Benches
of Supreme Court of India in consonance with the Article 130, Constitutional of India.

the personnel and we are always at the receiving end where delays are attributed to the
Supreme Court or to the High Court. The amount which the Court collects as the court fees
goes to the Government, not even the half is given to the court. This is the problem.”

7.7 The total sanctioned strength of Supreme Court Judges is 31. However, out of 31, the present
strength of Judges is only 28. As regards to the personnel strength, the Supreme Court has got a
sanctioned strength of 2,034, out of which, 1,691 is the total working strength.
7.8 The Committee expresses its serious concern over the mounting of cases pending in
Supreme Court. In view of the submission made by the Registrar, Supreme Court to it, the
Committee urges the Government to conduct a comprehensive comparative study of the
working of the Supreme Court vis-à-vis the apex Courts of other countries in order to identify
the grey areas. Thereafter, the course of action to augment the institution may be laid down.
7.9 The National Court Management System (NCMS) reports that India has one of the
largest judicial systems in the world, with over 3 crore of cases and sanctioned strength of
some 18,871 judges. The present judge population ratio being 15.5 judges per million population
is grossly inadequate to dispense the justice in a reasonable time, which is also a reason for
the high pendency of cases. The Committee strongly recommends that the judge-population
ratio may be corrected by appointing more judges in Courts to reduce pendency and ensure
timely delivery of justice. In Committee’s view, timely delivery of justice would go a long way
in enforcing discipline in the society, improvement in the compliance of the laws and consequently
curbing corruption in the society which is quite high on the Governments agenda, today.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE — AT A GLANCE
1. It has been observed that the Ministry of Finance has substantially slashed the grants
allocation in the Non-Plan demands for grants of the Ministry. The expenditure in the Non-
Plan side can be anticipated, and therefore, the Committee recommends that all the three
Departments of the Ministry should make close monitoring of spending under the various
heads of the Non-Plan expenditure and make concerted efforts for further saving in view of
the technological advancements in Government work establishments that cut on the requirements
of man power and resources, compared to yester-years. The Committee hopes that with
modernization of offices, the Non-Plan expenditure of these Departments can be curtailed
further so as to enhance the Plan projections and undertake more progressive and developmental
schemes and projects. The Committee, however, does not advocate reduction in plan funds at
the cost of efficient office management and service delivery. [Para 2.10.]
2. As regards the Plan projections, the Committee appreciates that the Ministry of
Finance has allocated funds to the Ministry as sought by it. The schemes and projects proposed
to be undertaken by the Departments in 2013-14 are also commendable. The Committee
therefore, desires that the three Departments of the Ministry of Law and Justice should make
concerted efforts to realize the goals set by them for the financial year and closely monitor
the implementation of the schemes and projects funded by them. The Committee, however,
cautions the Departments that they should take a pro active stance in the execution and
realization of the goals under the schemes and projects of the spending units under their
administrative jurisdiction and not merely play the role of the fund disbursing agency. The
Committee is hopeful that the Plan side of the demands for grants of the Ministry will go a
long way in bringing about better delivery of services. [Para 2.11]

hopes that the programme will fill up the existing gaps in the education and empowerment of
the voters by creating awareness, especially among the rural, deprived and women in particular
so as to make the democracy more vibrant. However, the Committee feels that the actual
target of voters awareness programme should be clearly defined so that the countries valuable
resources do not go waste. It should accordingly, implement the programme in a pre-determined
phased manner beginning with States nearer to elections. [Para 3.8]
4. Another important area of concern is the use of EVMs in the elections. An elector has
every right to know whether the candidate to whom he has cast his vote through the electronic
voting machine has actually gone for that candidate. This is not possible in the present system.
The Election Commission has reported that they are in the process of attaching printer to the
EVM on a limited scale for giving a printed copy of the vote cast by the elector at the polling
station. The Committee appreciates the initiatives taken by the Election Commission of India
to give a printed confirmation of the vote he has cast for the candidate of his/her choice to
confirm that no manipulation in the voting machine has occurred after the vote has been cast
by the elector. The Committee hopes that this measure of the Election Commission would go
a long way in establishing the faith of the electors in the EVMs and the processes in the
conduct of the elections. [Para 3.9]

56. The Committee expresses its serious concern over the mounting of cases pending in
Supreme Court. In view of the submission made by the Registrar, Supreme Court to it, the
Committee urges the Government to conduct a comprehensive comparative study of the
working of the Supreme Court vis-à-vis the apex Courts of other countries in order to identify
the grey areas. Thereafter, the course of action to augment the institution may be laid down.
[Para 7.8]
57. The National Court Management System (NCMS) reports that India has one of the
largest judicial systems in the world, with over 3 crore of cases and sanctioned strength of
some 18,871 judges. The present judge to population ratio being 15.5 judges per million
population is grossly inadequate to dispense the justice in a reasonable time, which is also a
reason for the high pendency of cases. The Committee strongly recommends that the judge-
population ratio may be corrected by appointing more judges in Courts to reduce pendency and
ensure timely delivery of justice. In Committees view, timely delivery of justice would go a
long way in enforcing discipline in the society, improvement in the compliance of the laws and
consequently curbing in corruption in the society which is quite high on the Governments
agenda, today. [Para 7.9]
