1
REPORT
India is the home to large number of tribal Communities. The tribal population of the
country, as per 2011 census, is 104281034, constituting 8.61 percent of the total population
(1210569573) which inhabit in 15 percent of the geographical area of the country. The total
recognised tribes in the country listed in the First Schedule to the Constitution (Scheduled Tribe)
Order, 1950 is 698. Out of 698 recognised tribes in the country, as many as 31 tribes have more
than five lakh population
1. Broadly, the tribal communities inhabit in two distinct geographical areas
of the country- the Central India and the North-Eastern Region 2. However, except Assam, the ratio
of State-wise population of Scheduled Tribes to total population of States is highest in the North-
Eastern States. The percentage of Scheduled Tribes population to total population of the State on
North Eastern Region is 94.4 % in Mizoram, 86.5% in Nagaland, 86.1% in Meghalaya, 68.8% in
Arunachal Pradesh, 35.1% in Manipur, 33.8% in Sikkim, 31.8% in Tripura and 12.4% in Assam.
CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISIONS FOR SCHEDULED TRIBES IN NORTH-EASTERN REGION
2. Constitution of India provides protection to indigenous tribal communities and their customs
through Articles 244, 244-A and 371A (Nagaland) and 371G (Mizoram). Article 366 (25) defines
Scheduled Tribes as "such tribes or tribal communities or parts of or groups within such tribes or
tribal communities as are deemed under Article 342 to be Scheduled Tribes for the purposes of this
Constitution". Article 342 provides for specification of tribes or tribal communities or parts of or
groups within tribes or tribal communities which are deemed to be for the purposes of the
Constitution the Scheduled Tribes in relation to that State or Union Territory. In pursuance of these
provisions, the list of Scheduled Tribes are notified for each State or Union Territory and are valid
only within the jurisdiction of that State or Union Territory and not outside. The areas where tribal
populations are preponderance are called Scheduled Areas and Tribal Areas in the country.
3. The Fifth Schedule of Constitution applies to tribal communities of Central India, while the
Sixth Schedule applies to certain tribal communities of North-Eastern Region. The  Sixth  Schedule
of the Constitution operates  in  parts  of  Assam,  Mizoram  and  Tripura  and  throughout  the
State  of Meghalaya, except Shillong. The Schedule provides for administration of certain tribal
areas as autonomous entities, wherein the administration of autonomous district and region is to be
vested in District and Regional Councils in these areas which have a long tradition of self
management and governance systems. The Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996
(PESA) has been made applicable to Fifth Schedule areas. The Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 is also
made applicable to Fifth Schedule areas. Traditional Gram Sabhas inter-alia  have been given the
power to adjudicate in accordance with prevalent tradition and customs under PESA, 1996.  Both
PESA, 1996 and Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 are yet to be extended to North-Eastern States.
1
1 Bhil, Gond, Santhal, Mina, Naikada, Oraon, Sugalis, Munda, Naga, Kond, Boro, Koli Mahadev, Khasi, Kol, Varli, Kokna, Kawar,
Ho, Gujjar, Korku, Bhumij, Garo, Koya, Mizo (Lushai) Tribes, Halba, Dharua, Dubla, Mishing, Tripuri, Rathawa, Saharia.
2 Statistical Profile of Scheduled Tribes in India, 2013 . Statistical Division, Ministry of Tribal Affairs (P.3)

2
DISPUTE RESOLUTION SYSTEM IN SCHEDULE/TRIBAL AREAS OF NORTH-EASTERN
REGION
4. Para 4 of the Sixth Schedule to Constitution envisages Customary Village Council/Court in
respect of law enacted under paras 3 and 4 of the Schedule where both the parties are Scheduled
Tribe of such area. Para 5 of the Sixth Schedule confers powers to District Councils to try suits
and cases under Civil Procedure Court and Criminal Procedure Court. The Customary Village
Councils/Courts are generally manned by chieftain of the tribe/clan and are assisted by Village
Council comprising village elders. It adjudicates disputes of petty nature relating to property,
matrimonial disputes, house trespass, theft, etc. the punishment is in terms of fine (mithun or
cash). There is no system of imprisonment/jail in the customary judicial system. The hearings are
publicly conducted in the presence of parties and village elders and punishments are swiftly
awarded. They follow their uncodified customary laws and are locally known as Goan Buras  in
Arunachal Pradesh, Cheirap (civil) and Garot (military court) amongst some tribes of Manipur and
Dobhasis  in Nagaland, etc.
5. The regular justice system following Civil Procedure Code and Code of Criminal Procedure
Code also simultaneously exists in North-Eastern Region which are manned by members of judicial
services. The customary Village Council/Court as well as regular court system is under the
superintendence of High Court of concerned State under Article 235 of Constitution. The parties to
the disputes have option for going to higher courts for appeal.
6. Tribal justice system and regular justice system are different in their structure and
approach. The modern legal system is largely based on the English Common Law and is
characterised by uniform territorial rules, based on universal principles of natural justice and is
administered by a hierarchy of courts. This system has regular and affirmed methods of revisiting
and revising its rules and procedures. Whereas, the traditional systems of justice are largely un-
codified, comprise of overlapping jurisdictions enjoying autonomy in administration of justice. Due
to the diversity among the tribal groups, each tribe in India has its unique socio-cultural milieu and
dispute resolution practices and which have remained unchanged over generations
3.
7. In Scheduled and Tribal Areas, the preference of people to the tribal justice system is quite
high as compared to the formal justice system of Courts. Due to expensive and dilatory procedures
of courts, they fail to become the endpoints for justice for the marginalised. Therefore, traditional
or customary institutions for resolution of disputes have been recognised through legislative
instruments in several States
4.
8. Article 13(3) of the Constitution of India has clearly recognized custom as a source of law.
Customs are recognised as a measure of laws if that is immemorial in origin, reasonable in nature
and continuous in use and in conformity with the provisions of the Constitution. In U Fairly Syiem
Vs. Khasi Hills Autonomous District Council ( Writ Petition No. 5866 of 2006 (PS) Guwahati High
Court) to the election of Syiem or administrative head of the Nongstoin, the custom as codified by
the Khasi Hills Autonomous District (Nomination and Election of the Syiem, Deputy Syiem and
Electors of Nongstoin Syiemship) Act, 2003 and Nongstoin Syiemship Rules, 2003 was relied upon
3 Background Note on the subject supplied by Department of Justice, Ministry of Law and Justice.
4 Ibid

3
to uphold the election of Syiem. In Ruiweinao Kahaosan Tangkhul Vs. Rueiweinao Simirei (AIR
1961 Manipur 1) the court held that the custom of offering one day free labour in a year to the
village head contained elements of compulsion which is void under Article 23 of the Constitution of
India
5.
9. National Commission for Women in its Report on Customary Laws in North-East India:
Impact on Women (2007) submitted that:
"…In the North-east many tribes continue to regulate themselves according to their own
customary laws while most laws of the Middle India tribes fell by the wayside because of
the onslaught of the pan-Indian laws. Among many hill tribes of this region the village
chief regulates the use of land and water and has administrative and judicial power. …The
tribes combine kinship based political organisation with well-defined laws and procedures
for punishment of offenders through traditional courts. ….
6"
10. Justice Madan B. Lokur of Supreme Court of India in his Lecture Series on Tribal and
Customary Laws (2013) opined that:
"....The system of enforcement of tribal customs is very strong in the North-East and is
constitutionally protected. Conventional courts, as we understand them, are very often out
of reach for tribals in the North-East and that is another reason why the method of
dispensing justice in accordance with customary law is so popular among the tribals.... it is
necessary for all of us to try and strengthen customary courts and enforcement of customary
laws amongst the tribal communities since that system of administration of justice has been
accepted and practised by them for centuries without any dissatisfaction with their justice
delivery system
7.
CODIFICATION OF CUSTOMARY LAW OF THE TRIBES
11. The first prerequisite for an effective synergy between the tribal justice system and the
regular justice system is the dedicated effort at codification of customary law of tribal communities
in the region. At present a large body of tribal laws in the North-Eastern region is oral in nature
which is committed to the memory of a few key individuals in the village. A few attempts are being
made by academic and a research institutions to codify the law. One among them is Law Research
Institute, Guwahati. In Jharkhand, the customary laws on tenurial rights over land have been
documented for Munda tribe, in the Chota Nagpur Tenancy Act, 1908. Similarly, in Meghalaya  and
Nagaland, customary village courts have been documented in Administration of Justice Rules, 1953
of Meghalaya and the Nagaland Village and Area Councils Act, 1978.
12. The Committee in its Twenty-sixth Report on Demands for Grants (2008-09) of Ministry of
Law and Justice has observed that:
"….Though, there were no written rules for administration of tribal villages, but the
customs and traditions were almost compatible with the modern concepts of jurisprudence.
5 As cited In Lokur, Justice Madan B. 2013. Customary Laws And Good Governance, Lecture Series on Tribal And Customary Laws.
Ranchi, Central University of Jharkhand (P . 16-17).
6 Fernandes, Walter, Melville Pereira And Vizalenu Khatso, 2007. Customary Laws In North-East India: Impact on Women . New
Delhi: National Commission for Women.  (P.24). http://ncw.nic.in/pdfreports/Customary%20law.pdf
7 Lokur, Justice Madan B, 2013. Customary Laws and Good Governance , Lecture Series on Tribal and Customary Laws, Ranchi.
Central University of Jharkhand (P .36).

4
The tribal councils in North-East State were functioning on the lines of the system evolved
for parliamentary democracy, which is in vogue now a days. The council derived their
authority from the expression of the will and power of the people. They had the support of
both social and supernatural. Thus the concept of parliamentary democracy is not new to
the tribal society
8.
DEPOSITION OF SECRETARY, DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE
13. The Secretary, Department of Justice in her deposition submitted that the Subject 'Synergy
between Tribal Justice System and Regular Justice System of the Country' is actually not part of
their mandate.  The Department of Justice stated that the practices under the tribal justice system
are un-codified, customary and varies from tribe to tribe. Certain provisions in the Constitution of
India and some special laws, however, recognise the tribal customary practices and also the
existence and role of community participation in disputes resolution. The Fifth and Sixth Schedules
of the Constitution provide for administration of tribal areas in notified States. Special Constitutional
provisions under Article 371 have been provided for North-Eastern States.  Dispute adjudication as
per traditions and customs has been provided for in the Panchayat (Extension to Scheduled Areas)
Act, 1996 and Scheduled Tribe and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest
Rights) Act, 2006. The customary institutions are preferred places for the dispute resolution and
institutions of Gaon Buras  are recognized in certain North-Eastern States. The Rules for the
Administration of Justice and Police in Nagaland framed under Scheduled District Act, 1874, as
amended in 1984 has brought about synergy between the tribal and regular justice system where
the customary courts try cases between parties belonging to Scheduled Tribes.
DEPOSITION OF SECRETARY, MINISTRY TRIBAL AFFAIRS
14. The Secretary submitted that the Ministry has nothing to do with tribal justice system.  He
averred that Ministry of Tribal Affairs is essentially concerned with governance issues in tribal area
under Fifth Schedule of the Constitution. He added that as per allocation of Business Rules, 1961
administration of justice, access to justice and justice delivery system are allocated to Department
of Justice.  There is neither a division nor any record of past experience with the Ministry for
dealing with the subject.
15. Ministry of Tribal Affairs further submitted that Village Panchayat/Council of Tribal
communities residing in Fifth Schedule areas do not exercise judicial power while those residing in
Sixth Schedule areas have judicial powers. Since customary tribal laws are a sort of oral tradition,
codification thereof is a tough challenge for the State. There have been allegations that village heads
have reportedly used those customary laws prejudicially in favour of their relatives and
acquaintances. He submitted that customary tribal law should be in conformity with principle of
natural justice and need to be synchronised with regular justice system to check its misuse.
SUGGESTIONS RECEIVED FROM STATE GOVERNMENTS OF NORTH-EASTERN STATES
16. The Committee then sent a questionnaire to the Secretary, Department of Justice with a
view to obtain written views of the Law Secretaries of the tribal dominated States of the Country.
8 Twenty-sixth Report on Demands for Grants (2008-09) of Ministry of Law and Justice presented to Parliament on 29th April,
2008 (P . 76).

5
Accordingly, replies/comments of the North-Eastern States of Meghalaya, Mizoram, Tripura,
Nagaland, Manipur, Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh have been received.
17. The State Government of Meghalaya submitted that the State falls under the Sixth Schedule
of the Constitution. Village Courts are in existence in all the villages headed by headman in East
Khasi Hills, Doloi's in Jainitia Hills and Nokmas/Sordars/Laskar in Garo Hills under Rules 2(k), 5
and 6 of the Administration of Justice Rules, 1953. An appeal from these courts lies with the
Syiem's/District Council Courts and High Court. On the issue of codification of customary laws, the
State Government submitted that only those customary laws that are practised generally have been
codified by the respective District Councils. The Customary laws which are localised and varies
from village to village are in the process of codification.
18. The State Government of Mizoram submitted that there is no conflict between tribal justice
system and regular justice system in the State. The Justice System existing in the Sixth Schedule
Areas (rural Mizoram) does not violate the Indian Constitution and the laws made thereunder.
19. The State Government of Tripura submitted that majority of tribal people in the State are
guided by community based customary laws and as a result tribal peoples' participation in the
regular justice system of the State judiciary for settlement of disputes is very low. Tribal
communities such as Jamatias have hierarchal dispute resolution mechanisms which may or may
not involve the mainstream courts. Only heinous cases come to the regular courts through police
stations.  In the tradition bound tribal society the law of the statute book does not command the
respect which the dictum of the village elders does. The State Government has requested to do
away with the customary laws which are repugnant to the concept of natural justice and
fundamental rights and at the same time adopting customary laws which are reasonable and
beneficial to the interests of larger society.
20. The State Government of Nagaland submitted that under Article 371A of the Constitution
safeguard is provided for administration of both civil and criminal justice according to Naga
customary laws. The Rules of Administration of Justice and Police in Nagaland, 1937 provide for
administration of justice according to customary laws and procedures. The criminal justice
continues to be administered by the Village Courts at the village level, at the Dubashi's  Court on
appeals and thereafter the Assistant to Deputy Commissioner and the High Courts. Under the 1937
rules there are no specific provisions for recording of proceedings during trials which are
conducted through viva voce , which pose a problem for higher courts during the appeal stage.
Accordingly, the Customary Courts are being sensitised to record proceedings and judgements. The
separation of judiciary from executive has been commenced in Dimapur district which are being
extended to other districts. In Dimapur due to mixed population of various Naga tribes, customary
laws differ from tribe to tribe so litigants prefer to approach statutory courts under regular
mainstream statutes.
21. The State Government of Sikkim submitted that no area in the State of Sikkim has been
included or declared as Scheduled Area as per the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution. The concept
of tribal justice system does not exist and the judicial system in the State involving the
administration of justice covers and applies uniformly to all individuals, tribals and non-tribals.
However, the State Government made an attempt for ascertaining and codification of customary

6
laws of the different ethnic communities in the State and accordingly, the Law Commission of
Sikkim under the Chairmanship of Justice D. M. Sen submitted report on Sikkim Customary Laws.
However, due to divergent views on different subjects  and lack of uniformity it was not found
feasible for codification.
22. The State Government of Manipur submitted that no area of the State is a Scheduled Area
under the Constitution of India. The customary laws are not in use and statutory laws are followed
in all areas of the State and also there is no specific Acts, Rules etc. which incorporate tribal laws.
However, for legislating laws relating to inheritance of property, marriage and divorce, the same has
to be done in consultation with the Hill Areas Committee of the Manipur Legislative Assembly in
terms of the Presidential order of 1972 promulgated under the Article 371C of the Constitution of
India.
23. The State Government of Arunachal Pradesh submitted that tribes in the State have distinct
customary laws and traditional institutions for administrating justice. These administrations
administer both civil and criminal justice. At higher level, there is separation of powers between
judiciary and executive, however, due to inadequacy of regular courts the traditional justice system
of the tribes fill the gap at lower levels. The indigenous institutions are more democratic,
participatory, simple, cost effective and expeditious and have prevented the accumulation of
pendency of cases. The State Government has further submitted that there is an urgent need to
make special provisions akin to Articles 371A and 371G , respectively, meant for Nagaland and
Mizoram.
24.   In response to Committee's query viz., whether any efforts have been made by the respective
State Government's to synergise the tribal system with the regular judicial system, the State

SUGGESTIONS RECEIVED FROM STAKEHOLDERS
27. Suggestions received from Tribal leaders, Autonomous District Councils and other
Stakeholders during the study-visit of the Committee to Shillong and Guwahati from 31st October

7
to 6th November, 2015:-
(a) The State Government of Assam submitted that the State Government have enacted
two Acts (i) The Assam Administration of Justice in Karbi Anglong District Act,
2009, and (ii) The Assam Administration of Justice in North Cachar Hills District
Act, 2009 to administer both civil and criminal justice in the above mentioned tribal
areas by setting up courts.
(b) Shri Melvil Pereira of North-Eastern Social Research Centre, Guwahati submitted
that Tribal customary law is an important part of tribal societies. They are not just
a matter of jurisprudence but a part of their culture. It is a visible expression of
values, ideals and principles a particular culture upholds. It is followed because it is
convenient, conducive and helpful to society as it reflects societal norms and values.
Most tribes in the region live according to their customary law. In North-East India,
many tribes have documented and compiled their customary laws ( e.g. Angamis in
Nagaland). Customary Laws need to be made gender sensitive in case of
participation, property and maintenance keeping in view of the Fundamental Rights
contained in the Part III of the Constitution. The appointment of young Gaon Bura
and Dobashis  who are not well versed in the tribal customary law has resulted in
public losing its faith in the customary law. In 2005, Government of Nagaland
announced its plan for a single customary law for the entire State.
(c) Representatives of Karbi Anglong Autonomous District Council submitted that Karbis
have their own traditional self-governing institutions. The Traditional system of
governance is monarchical in nature, whereby the king or Lindokpo  is at the apex
and followed by these traditional Habai (Head of region) and Sarthe (Head of the
village). The King has to attend all the social matters and settle disputes referred by
the Habais and  Lindokpos . The Karbis also have a traditional bachelors' dormitory
locally known as Riso Ateriang  and Jirkedam, which acts as a training centre for
social activities under the leadership of chiefs.
(d) Representatives of Singpo Tribe submitted that the Singpo society maintains its
customary law in its day to day activities and only in exceptional cases it is referred
to the Police State/Magistrate. According to the Singpos, the process of delivering
justice through customary law is more accurate and amicable. Singpo community is
based on the chieftainship system and the Chief, who is called Mung Du , rules the
clan. Below him there are various other leaders hierarchically arranged. Disputes are
of the community are first tried by Mare Agi  or the village Headman and thereafter,
it moves up in the hierarchy if it is not resolved at lower level. The final decision on
a dispute is decided by the Mung Du  with the help of his council members.
(e) Representatives of Rabha Hasong Autonomous Council submitted that the customary
laws of Rabhas are institution which enforces faithful observance of the rules of
conduct approved by the society. These laws are meant for the maintenance of
social order and harmony and are found on the matters like matrimonial customs,
divorce, birth and death customs, religious customs, adoption, village council and so

8
on. Council of elders is the most powerful body in village councils and they have
both executive and judicial powers. All inter village disputes, social and customary
issues are dealt by council of elders.
(f) Representatives of Tiwa society submitted that the Tiwa (also known as lalung)
have their own judiciary system which owes its origin to their kings/chiefs. The
customary law is prevalent in both religious and social sphere. There are three tier
system of justice, i.e., Khel  (lowest level), Village level and Baro Khelia Bichar
system, which is most powerful system of justice delivery. If all three levels fail to
settle dispute, the matter is brought before the king whose decision is final. There is
also provision of Jury system, wherein Tiwa judiciary system consists of three
members to decide a dispute. Some of the important features of the customary law
are, viz., no corporal punishment and no death penalty and different types of penalty
imposed in accordance with the gravity of the offence.
(g) Representatives of Hima (Khasi) Tribes of Meghalaya submitted that Syiemships/
Lyngdohship/Sirdarships are in existence since time immortal and are headed by
Chiefs (Syiems/Lyngdohs/Sirdars)  are also recognised and protected by the Sixth
Schedule of the Constitution and they exercise all powers and functions through the
Durbar . The Hima had its origin in the tribal organisation of the Khasis
encompassing civil, judicial and administrative matters. The Hima requested the
Committee that certain provisions in Sixth Schedule may be included to preserve its
control of land, forest and resources of the community. They further requested that
Constitutional recognition be given to Village Durbars/Village Councils and Traditional
Institutions, which are the grass-root governance system with administrative and
judicial powers.
(h) Dr. O. D Valentina Ladia, Advocate, High Court of Meghalaya submitted that in the
pre-colonial times the Khasi Syiems  had both civil and criminal powers. It also had
both original and appellate jurisdiction. The decision of the chief was final. Under
the British Rule, the tribal customary laws and practices were preserved till the year
1858 and thereafter, some changes were brought by orders/notifications by the
British Government in India. The Jainitias (Pnars) like the Khasis had similar system
of administration. However, the system differed from that of Kahsis due to
difference in the organisation of Jainitia State. The Durbar exercised executive,
legislative and judicial functions in the Jainitia State. Among the Garos, people
belonging to the clan lived in a village known as Akhing Land . Each Village had a
chief and people owed allegiance to Chief called Nokma , who exercised
administrative, executive and judicial functions. After independence, Khasi Syiemship
Administration of Justice Order, 1950 was passed which vested the administration of
justice with the Deputy Commissioner. Hierarchy of Courts was established under
the Administration of Justice Rule, 1950 (Village Courts, Subordinate, Additional
Subordinate and District Courts). There is no limit of the pecuniary jurisdiction of
the Courts, but limitation on power with respect to criminal courts. Against the
judgments of the District Courts, appeals lie with the High Courts.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
28. The committee observes that due to their familiarity with customary laws, most of
the tribal communities in the Sixth Schedule areas prefer tribal justice system based on
customary practices  over the regular justice system. Furthermore, the tribal justice system
involves minimal procedure and is cost effective and ensure timely delivery of justice. Those
customary Village Council/Courts in North Eastern Region are headed by tribal chief and
assisted by village elders and highly respected. But the presence of multiplicity of tribal
groups in each North-Eastern State, the customary practices of dispute resolution vary from
one tribal group to another even in the same State. The judicial process and
pronouncements followed by tribes in the region are oral in tradition, which provide wide
room for discretion to the tribal chief during the justice delivery system, sometimes leading
to award of different punishment for crime of similar nature.
29. The Committee could come to the conclusion after discussing elaborately that Tribal
Justice system needs to be brought by separate legislation in the Parliament with liberty to
States to amend, add or modify according to the need of the particular State. Such law
should give institutional support in the name of 'Tribal Justice Court' system with flexibility
of appointing presiding officer and staff from existing personnel without insisting on tenure,
age, education, and other matters. But the salary and facilities should be equal to First class
Magistrate-cum-Civil Judge/District Munsif as recognised by the Criminal Code of
Procedure or Civil Procedure Code as entry level Judicial officers. This would enable them
to be financially benefited and help them to organise themselves for codifying and writing
judgments and orders, following penal laws and precedents. This aspect of training can be
done by making provision of special funding to State Judicial Academy and Village Mobile
courts to encourage the States and High Courts to implement with enthusiasm. The
recognition can be in the line of Lok Adalat Court system recognised by Parliament
enactment to be manned by retired Judge, laymen other members of the court with powers
under Chapter VI and VI (A) of National Legal Services Authorities Act 1987. Moreso
mediation, conciliation and arbitration are the tools for success in that system with no
appeals to higher courts. Till tribal law is matured enough to be codified these tools will be
at the disposal of the Customary tribal courts. Criminal code, and Civil code can be
amended by concerned State Governments. When this committee recommended to establish
separate High Courts for North Eastern States in Twenty Sixth Report on Demands for
Grants (2008-09) of Ministry of Law and Justice presented to Parliament on 29th April,
2008, the then Government was hesitant since tribal judicial system may not allow to have
enough cases for the High Court. But Meghalaya High Court has recently suggested to the
to Committee to increase the number of Judges of that Court from 2 to 3 as huge pendency
of cases are to be cleared. Hence the tribal justice system has to be allowed to be
synchronised with regular Justice system at the root level so that judge-made law will give
energy to bring statutory law.
30. The Committee notes that the main reasons for the avoidance of regular judicial
system by the tribal people in certain pockets of the country is due to expensive, lengthy
and confusing procedural laws and lengthy procedures of the regular Courts. The Committee

10
feels that non exposure of large number of tribal people to regular justice system has
forced large number of them to remain out of the ambit of mainstream justice delivery
system prevailing in the country. The Committee while recognising the contribution of
customary practices of tribes in dispensation of justice, feels that benefits of regular justice
system should not be denied to tribal people.
31.  The Committee strongly feels that the respective State Governments have to initiate
the process of synergising the two. Firstly, they have to allay the apprehension from the
minds of the people that they would lose the benefits of tribal justice system and  instil the
faith that it would rather strengthen it.  Secondly, they should also make available the
necessary infrastructure, competent and trained judicial officers through its judicial
academies, and also by introducing modern record management practices.  The services of
State Legal Services Authorities at States and Districts level may be utilised in the region to
remove the skepticism and reservations among the tribal people in the region about the
regular justice system. The Committee is not at all for replacement of customary justice
delivery mechanism with the regular system but is of the view that these two systems
instead of being compartmentalised should converge in a symbiotic manner to enhance
access to justice to those indigenous inhabitants.
32. The Committee observes that in contrast to the general perception of egalitarian
nature of tribal societies, women in many tribal societies are not permitted to participate in
public offices and their property rights are also restricted. The Committee feels that
representation of women in the tribal bodies and district councils may be encouraged by
consultation and legislative process to bring gender equality in the local administration as
provided under the Part IX of the Constitution in the Panchayat Raj Institutions.
33. The Committee observes that at present there are large bodies of tribal laws which
are oral in tradition and transmitted from generation to generation. A few attempts have
been made in Nagaland among Ao and Zelang Tribes  and in Assam among Bodos to document
and codify their customary laws. The Committee also recognises the efforts of Law
Research Institute, Guwahati in documenting customary law in the North-East region.  The
Committee feels that such efforts need to be encouraged in the region for documentation
and finally codification of diverse customary laws prevalent among various tribes in the
region. The Committee is of the view that a careful examination of the similarities/
dissimilarities between the regular and tribal justice system of the country is the need of
the hour so that the tribal laws can be documented and codified and a synergy can be
brought with the regular justice system as oral traditions sometimes leads to arbitrary
dispensation of justice and violates the principle of natural justice and rights provided under
the Constitutional of India.  This can be undertaken in the project Access to Justice for
North-East and Jammu and Kashmir which is currently being implemented by Department
of Justice.
34. The Committee feels that efforts can also be made to provide training and building
capacities of traditional/customary judicial officials, Gaon Buras , Cheirups , Dobashish  etc. on
the principles of natural justice in the State Judicial Training Academies. The Committee
feels that training and infrastructure should be provided to State Judicial Academies to train

11
tribal leaders, chief of Gaon Buras  etc.  so as to apprise them of the benefits of regular
justice system and integrate them to regular justice system of the Country, ultimately,
bringing about a synergy between both these systems for the development and good
governance of Tribal Areas in the country. The financial implications of these training
programmes and empowerment activities need to be worked out by the respective
authorities.
35. As per the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, administration
of justice, access to justice, justice delivery system  and legal aid to poor falls under the
purview of Department of Justice, Ministry of Law and Justice and Tribal Welfare,
Development of Scheduled Tribes and Scheduled Areas falls under the purviews of the
Ministry of Tribal Affairs. The Committee during its deliberations with the Departments and
Ministries of the Government of India on the subject observed that the issue of tribal
justice system in the country has not been taken seriously by the Department of Justice or
Ministry of Tribal Affairs for the reason that the issue does not specifically fall within their
domain as per (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961. The Committee feels that at apex level
it is the Department of Justice endowed with the responsibility of administration of justice
and accordingly expect that department to initiate the process of synergising both the
justice delivery systems and coordinate with the concerned State Governments, Tribal
Councils and other stakeholders.
36. The Committee in its Twenty Sixth Report on Demands for Grants (2008-09) of
Ministry of Law and Justice, presented to Parliament on 29th April, 2008 had recommended
for establishing separate High Courts for North Eastern States which will in turn play the
role of evolving codification of the tribal laws. It had felt that such a step would ensure that
the judgements of the High Courts will be treated as precedents, which with passage of
time, can evolve into written law. The interpretations given to the existing uncodified rules/
laws by the High Courts, can in future, be consolidated and this will result in codified laws
and uniformity of judgements. This Committee now reiterates that all the North Eastern
States should have separate High Courts and independent Judicial Academy should be
established in every State to fulfil the real goal of synchronisation of Tribal Justice system
with the National mainstream of unitary Judicial system which is the architecture of Indian
Constitution.

special laws, however, recognize the tribal customary practices and also the existence and role of

would help to recognize customary tribal laws in these States.  Thereafter, Secretary, Tribal Affairs
made a presentation supplemented by his Joint Secretary.
4. The Secretary submitted that the Forest Rights Act basically relates to customary land rights
of tribals and has nothing to do with tribal justice system. He averred that Ministry of Tribal Affairs
is essentially concerned with governance issues in tribal area under Fifth Schedule of the
Constitution. He added that as per Allocation of Business Rules, 1961 administration of justice,
access to justice and justice delivery system are allocated to Department of Justice. The subject
matter of synergy between tribal justice system and regular justice system in the country is
subsumed under that mandate. There is neither a division nor any record of past experience with
the Ministry for dealing with the subject. Therefore, he opposed transfer of this subject to his
Ministry from Department of Justice.
5. The Joint Secretary in Ministry of Tribal Affairs added that Village Panchayat/Council of
Tribal communities residing in Fifth Schedule areas do not exercise judicial power while those
residing in Sixth Schedule areas have judicial powers. Since customary tribal laws are a sort of oral
tradition, codification thereof is a tough challenge for the State. There have been allegations that
village heads have reportedly used those customary laws prejudiciously in favour of their relatives
and acquaintances. He submitted that customary tribal law should be in conformity with principle
of natural justice and need to be synchronized with regular justice system to check its misuse.
6. Members pointed out that inspite of Forest Rights Act having overriding effect over other
existing laws, the Forest Department are coming in the way of implementation Forest Rights of
tribals.  The Tribal Village Panchayat have not been involved in the process. Tribal people cannot
mortgage their land resources to get bank loan for their economic development. The problem of
rehabilitation of displaced tribal population due to mining operation need to be looked into.
(After the arrival of the non-official witnesses)

22
7. The Chairman welcomed Shri H.S. Thangkhiew, Senior Advocate, High Court of Meghalaya,
Shri John F. Kharshing, Co-Chariman, Meghalaya State Planning Board and Prof. Nandini Sundar,
University of Delhi to the meeting. He requested the non-official witnesses to present their views
on the subject 'Synergy between Tribal Justice System and Regular Justice System of the Country'.
8. Shri H.S. Thangkhiew, Advocate, submitted that three prominent tribes ( Khasi, Jaintias  and
Garos) inhabitating in the hills of Meghalaya have their age old system of dispute resolution where
the decisions are taken up by consensus from village level to the chief of the tribe.  Rules for the
Administration of Justice framed in 1937 had recognized the role of village councils/courts and
village headman in the dispensation of justice amongst tribes. The Constitution under Sixth Schedule
has given power to Autonomous District Councils for constituting village courts/councils for trial of
suits amongst tribes, appointment/succession village headman, tribal customs etc., for disposal of
cases between them. The Administration of Justice Rules enacted in 1953 also recognized village
courts, District Councils but those are not functioning properly due to lack of finance and
infrastructure.  He, therefore, suggested that financial resources may be granted to the District
Council by the State Government for making it vibrant. The Transfer of Property Act, Specific
Reliefs Act should be made applicable in the scheduled areas. Village headman should be given
training in judicial processes by the State to resolve disputes in judicious manner.
9. Shri John F. Kharshiing referred to the Instrument of Acession entered into between some
of the Khasi Chiefs and Government of India, but that has not been mentioned in the Constitution
of India. However, none of the Chiefs are part of legislature and they are dependent for legislation
on the District Council which is a party-based body whereas the Chiefs are partyless institutions.
He submitted that ninety percent people in Meghalaya register their land with the Chiefs and not in
accordance with the Indian Registration Act, 1908. About eighty percent of cases in Meghalaya
goes to District Council for redressal of their grievances but those lack financial resource and
infrastructure to deal with the burden of cases. On the issue of codification of customary laws, he
opined that sometimes there is a conflict between the customary laws and the regular justice
system and felt that there is a need for synergy between them.
10. Prof. Nandini Sundar submitted that situation in Sixth Schedule areas are much better than
the Fifth Scheduled areas as far as the preservation of traditional justice systems is concerned. The
Y ule Rules, Santhal Police Rules and Pargana Majhi Rules in tribal areas of Central India allow the
tribals some degree of autonomy to preserve customary laws. But implementation of Panchayats
(Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act 1996 (PESA) had eroded such system. She added that the
customary practices needed to be recognized and revived. She apprised the Committee of the denial
of rights to tribal women in the traditional and customary laws. She also added that the complicated
procedures of formal legal system pushes the Adivasis towards to legal system delivered by Maoist,
where the justice delivery is quick and effective.
11. Members sought clarification on certain issues arising out of the presentations. The
witnesses responded to some of the queries and the Chairman directed them to give written
clarifications on issues not responded to during the interaction.

REPORT
A. Introductory Observation:
Treaties are frequently described as contracts between nations. As instruments of
International law, they establish obligations with which International law requires the parties to
comply at national level as well as international level. Entering into treaties and agreements with
foreign powers is one of the attributes of State sovereignty. The Vienna Convention of Law of
Treaties is the main instrument that regulates treaties. Article 2(1)(a) of the Vienna Convention of
Law of Treaties defines treaties as an international agreement concluded between States in written
form and governed by International Law, whether embodied in a single instrument or in two or
more related instruments and whatever its particular designation. The doctrine of pacta sunt
servanda  contained in articles 26 and 27 of the Vienna Convention, 1980 which lays down that
every treaty in force is binding upon the parties to it and must be performed in good faith.
2. The Consultation Paper under the auspices of National Commission to Review the Working
of the Constitution on topic of “Treaty Making Power under Our Constitution” begins with the
note, “ Entering into treaties and agreements with foreign powers is one of the attributes of State
sovereignty. No State can insulate itself from the rest of the world whether it be in the matter of
foreign relations, trade, environment, communications, ecology or finance. This is more true since
the end of the World War II. The advent of globalisation and the enormous advances made in
communication and information technology have rendered independent States inter-dependent. Every
State has entered into and is entering into treaties – be it multi-lateral or bilateral – which have a
serious impact upon the economy and the social and political life of its society. In spite of the
fundamental importance of the treaty-making power, it has unfortunately received very little
attention in our country, though in many other countries, good amount of research and debate has
gone into it .” (January 8, 2001) The above mentioned specific topic under the National
Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution was headed by Hon’ble Justice Shri B. P.
Jeevan Reddy.
B. Current Practice of Entering into International Treaties and the Executing Agencies
3. Article 51 of the Constitution of India enjoins the State to endeavour to “ foster respect for
international law and treaty obligations in the dealings of organised peoples with one another ”. For
the purpose of international relations and international obligations, the ‘State’ referred to in Article
51 is understood to be the Union of India, i.e. the Central Government. According to the
Constitutional arrangements, in particular Entries 10 and 14 of List 1 of the Union List in the
Seventh Schedule of the Constitution, all matters of foreign affairs which bring the Union into
relation with foreign countries including entering into treaties and agreements fall within the ambit
of the Union of India, the Central Government.
4. Under the Government of India (Allocation of the Business) Rules, 1961, as per Rule 3 of
the Second Schedule regarding ‘Distribution of subjects among the Departments’, the Ministry of

2
External Affairs has been entrusted the responsibility to negotiate Political treaties, agreements and
conventions with foreign and Commonwealth countries in various disciplines and subjects which
inter alia  include:
 matters relating to Law of the Sea, including the Indian Territorial Waters,
Contiguous Zone, Continental Shelf and Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZ);
 questions of international law arising on the high seas including fishery rights; piracy
and crimes committed on the High Seas or in the air;
 offences against the Law of Sovereign States committed on land or the High Seas or
in the air;
 legal matters concerning the International Seabed Area and Authority;
 United Nations, Specialised Agencies and other International Organisations and
Conferences;
 extradition and laws relating to extraditing of accused persons from India to foreign
and commonwealth countries and vice versa;
 demarcation of the land frontiers of India;
 maritime boundaries of India;
 human Rights law including: (a) interaction with Human Rights abroad; (b)
international declarations, treaties, conventions and conferences; (c) references
received from the United Nations and other specialised agencies and organisations
thereof; (d) implementation of reporting obligations, in coordination with the
concerned Ministries, required under the United Nations and international
conventions, to which India is a State party.
4.1 The same Rules has also allocated the subject “Treaties and agreements with foreign
countries in matters of civil law” to the Department of Legal Affairs, Ministry of Law & Justice.
5. The Committee has been informed by the Ministry of External Affairs that for discharging
its allocated functions and responsibilities in this regard, the Ministry has created the Legal and
Treaties Division in 1957 which is entrusted with the work relating to public international law. The
Division is approached for private international law work/issues by other Ministries and deals with
cases before the International Court of Justice and international arbitrations as well. The Division
also advises MEA and other Ministries/Departments of the Government of India on all issues of
international law including negotiations of treaties and agreements; and vetting of bilateral and
multilateral treaties/Memorandums of Understanding from international law angle.
6. As regards the role of the Department of Legal Affairs, Ministry of Law and Justice, it has
informed the Committee that the Department is primarily concerned with tendering of advice to
Ministries on legal matters including interpretation of the Constitution and the laws and conduct of
cases in the Supreme Court and the High Courts on behalf of the Central Government and on
behalf of the Governments of States participating in the Central Agency Scheme. It is also
concerned with reciprocal arrangements with foreign countries for the service of summons in civil

3
suits for the execution of decrees of Civil Courts, for the enforcement of maintenance orders, and
for the administration of the estates of foreigners dying in India.
7. The Department of Legal Affairs and Legislative Department (Ministry of Law) are required
to be consulted as per the Transaction of Business Rules on all Legislative proposals before the
proposal is brought before the Cabinet for approval. The Ministry does not deal with cases in
which legal opinion on questions of International Law or Treaties is sought by other Ministries
Departments in view of O.M.No.F.3(8)-O&M/61/1/152 dated the 30
th August, 1961 of the Ministry
of External Affairs which has requested that cases in which legal opinion on questions of
international law or treaties are required to be referred to the Legal and Treaties Division of the
Ministry of External Affairs.
8. The Department of Legal Affairs, however, in its advisory capacity is concerned with all
bilateral and multilateral treaties on legal issues and its impact on domestic law and examines the
Constitutional aspects irrespective of the subject allocation. The Department also examines issues
like clarity and formulation of provisions, legal implications of the Agreements, predominance of
domestic law in giving effect to the Agreement, presence of mechanism for interpretation and
implementation of the same and presence of Dispute Resolution Mechanism provided in the
Agreement. In the event of signing of any Treaty relating to the subjects related to different
Ministries, the concerned Ministry moves a Cabinet Note seeking concurrence from all the
Ministries/Departments concerned including Ministry of External Affairs and the Department of
Legal Affairs with the approval of its Minister.
9. In its written submission to the Committee, the Department of Legal Affairs has stated that
in number of instances, representatives of the Ministry of Law have not been involved at the time
of negotiating a draft Agreement and merely the negotiated draft Agreements were sent to this
Department for comments. It has suggested that representatives of the Department are made part
of the initial negotiations as well, so that legal implications of provisions are appropriately
understood and timely taken care of.
10. Whenever the Ministry of External Affairs comes across a situation while examining the
provisions of a Treaty that it has impact on the rights conferred by domestic law, it consults the
Department of Legal Affairs for opinion on the legal issues arising therein. The Department is also
consulted whenever in the process of negotiation or other matter with a foreign country involving
examination of any domestic legislation or any clarification on any domestic law issues with the
view of ensuring conformity with the relevant municipal laws and whenever any amendment in the
existing municipal law or an implementing legislation is required to fulfil the obligations assumed
under any international treaty/agreement.
C. Trends in Some Democratic Countries
11. In the United Kingdom, a practice was established whereby any treaty subject to ratification
is laid before Parliament for at least 21 sitting days before ratification is carried out, though
ratification being an executive power. Article II, Section 2 of the U.S. Constitution empowers the
President “ by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to make treaties, provided two-thirds
of the Senators present concur … ”. The President initiates and conducts negotiations of the treaties

4
and after signing them, places them before Senate for its “Advice and Consent”. In Australia,
treaties, both bilateral and multilateral are required to be tabled at least for 15 sitting days, after
signature but before they are ratified, to allow for parliamentary scrutiny. A joint Standing
Committee on treaties comprising Members of both Houses and consisting of Federal and State
Officers consider and report upon the treaties tabled before the House. The Canadian practice is
that, mandatory approval from the Parliament is required only in case of treaties that require
implementing legislation.
12. In New Zealand, the parliamentary treaty examination process introduced in 1997 and made
permanent in 2000 requires all multilateral treaties and major bilateral treaties of particular
significance to be presented to the House before binding treaty action is taken. In accordance with
the process, once Cabinet has approved the proposed treaty action, the Legal Division of the
Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade is responsible for presenting the treaty and the National
Interest Analysis to the House of the Representatives. Once a treaty has been presented, it stands
referred to the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee of the House.
D. Mandate to Indian Parliament to Give Effect to Treaties
13. Article 253 the constitution has empowered the Parliament to give effect to international law
treaties for the whole or any part the territory of India and reads:
“253. Legislation for giving effect to international agreements notwithstanding anything in
the foregoing provisions of this Chapter, Parliament has power to make any law for the
whole or any part of the territory of India for implementing any treaty, agreement or
convention with any other country or countries or any decision made at any international
conference, association or other body .”
14. In Maganbhai Ishwarbhai Patel vs. Union of India [(2002) 3 SCC], the Supreme Court
observed that “A treaty really concerns the political rather than the judicial wing of the State.
When a treaty or an award after arbitration comes into existence, if has to be implemented and this
can only be if all the three branches of Government, the Legislature, the Executive and the
Judiciary, or any of them, possess the power to implement it. If there is any deficiency in the
Constitutional system it has to be removed and the State must equip itself with the necessary
power.” Justice J.C. Shah observed in the aforesaid decision that “the effect of Article 253 is that
if a treaty, agreement or convention with a foreign State deals with a subject within the competence
of the State Legislature, the Parliament alone has, notwithstanding Article 246(3), the power to
make laws to implement the treaty, agreement or convention or any decision made at any
international conference, association or other body. In terms, the Article deals with legislative
power: thereby power is conferred upon the parliament which it may not otherwise possess.”
15. India adopts dualistic approach in relation to Treaties/Conventions which regards
international law and municipal law are separate in which one does not prevail over the other. India
follows the British practice as it existed at the time of its independence. States’ obligation to
domesticate its valid international obligations can be drawn from the Permanent Court of
International Justice (PCIJ) decision on Exchange of Greek and Turkish Populations Case , PCIJ
Reports, Series B, No. 10 (1925), 20. Also Article 27 of Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties
to which India is not yet a party (to the Vienna Convention 1969) provides that national law cannot

5
be invoked to justify non-compliance with international law. This approach entrusted major role to
Indian Parliament to ensure the implementation of international law and also to protect national
interest. This approach led the Indian Parliament to harmonise the international aspiration vs national
interest.
16. In February, 2000, the Ministry of Law and Justice set up the National Commission to
Review the Working of the Constitution to recommend functional changes which could be made to
the Constitution and parliamentary system in the light of socio-economic developments. The
Consultation Paper of the Commission gave two principal suggestions, i.e., (i) the Parliament must
make a law to regulate the treaty making power and; (ii)  the Union Government must consult with
States prior to signing any treaty in order to reduce conflicts with State Governments. The Second
Commission on Centre-State Relation headed by former Chief Justice of India M.M. Punchhi
recommended in its report in March, 2010 that in view of the vast and plenary nature of the
power, the Parliament should enact a law  to streamline the procedures involved in treaty-making.
While acknowledging that treaty-making involved complex, prolonged, multi-level issues which
could only be well handled by the executive, the Commission nevertheless felt that “Constitutional
mandate on federal governance cannot be ignored” .
17. In India, the Executive has been taking action on giving effect to treaties under Article 73
read with Entries 10 and 14 of list I of Seventh Schedule of the Constitution while Article 253 of
the Indian Constitution has empowered the Parliament to make any law for the whole or any part
of the territory of India for implementing any treaty, agreement or convention with any other
country or countries or any decision made at any international conference, association or other
body. The Ministry of External Affairs of the Government of India also issued a notification no. 1/
13/2/2010-Cab dated 2011, whereby accession to or ratification of such convention/treaties, be
undertaken only after relevant domestic laws have been amended, or the enabling legislation has
been enacted in cases, where there are no domestic laws on the subject.
18. The Indian Society of International Law submitted that use of resources and expertise of
Parliament and that Indian Parliament has to be involved in such matters in order to permit the law
to evolve and to develop properly. Views have also been expressed that the involvement of
Parliament could reduce the risk of inconsistent body of laws and help to legitimise and
institutionalise the process of inclusion of international law into domestic law and would aid in
making the system sustainable. Some Members likewise endorsed this view.
18.1 The Ministry of External Affairs also, in its written submission, acknowledged that
Parliament continues to exercise exclusive power in cases where implementing legislation may be
necessary to give effect to treaties, which may necessitate the adoption of the necessary legislation
by the Parliament before the treaty in question may be ratified and that Parliament has necessary
oversight over the treaty-making power of the Union Government.
E. Indian Courts and International Law
19. There has been a tremendous increase in standard setting/law making of international law on
various subjects bearing direct implications on India’s national interest. In the absence of any
domestic law, many of the cases in the Supreme Court are now finding that the international

6
treaties, conventions and agreements are enforced as it is. The treaty law raises many difficult
issues concerning the proper balance to be found between the international law and Indian domestic
law. The general ‘proliferation’ and increasing importance of treaty law, inter-governmental
organisation, international courts and tribunals introduce both substantive and procedural obligations
on States. The numerous International Courts and tribunals are continuously interpreting the
existing international law principles and expect that a State including India has to comply with those
interpretations. This requires a dedicated State institution to ensure that its laws and practice give
effect to these interpretations or to bring the national law in accordance with interpretations
provided by complex regime of international courts and tribunals.
20. There has been a couple of recent high profile examples of what can only be described as
inconsistent decisions in national and international judicial bodies. Many are concerned with
fundamental issues, viz., impairment of the friendly relations with other nations, principle of
peaceful co-existence, obligation of State trading partners, breach of international duty,  providing
effective remedy for violations of human rights and rule of law, non-discrimination provisions in
the WTO, freedom of the seas, common heritage of mankind, common concern of mankind,
delimitation of seas, freedom of navigation, peaceful exploration of outer space, etc. In brief, there
are a plethora of issues arising in respect of the co-existence of municipal and international courts
and remedies stemming out from the complex web of international law regime and the ever-
growing number of legal proceedings, both at national and international levels brought by States/
individuals against another State. Therefore, the relationship between local courts and international
law to give effect to the international law obligations poses a challenge.
21. The Department of Legal Affairs has also submitted that treaties do not become part of
Municipal law and Courts in India cannot interpret them unless Parliament enacts a legislation by
exercising power conferred under Article 253 of the Constitution read with Entry 14 of the List I
of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution in order to make it part of domestic law. As per the
existing norms, treaty is enforceable only when it is ratified by India after completing the
constitutional procedure.
22. The Supreme Court of India in Aban Loyd Chiles Offshore v. UOI (2008) 11 SCC 439)  held
that in the absence of municipal law, treaties can be looked into, if they are not in conflict with
municipal law. In Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan  ((1997) 6 SCC 241) and National Legal Services
Authority v. Union of India , ((2014) 5 SCC 438), the Supreme Court of India again applied
international law even when there was no municipal law. In T. N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v.
Union of India  ((2012) 4 SCC 362), the Supreme Court laid down a short but categorical directive
that treaties not contrary to municipal law are deemed to be incorporated in the municipal law. The
1969 and 1986 Vienna Conventions on the Law of Treaties between States and International
Organisations or between International Organisations mandate that their rules apply as binding
norms to the mutual relations entered into through Treaties/Covenants/Agreements.
23. There have been instances where Indian courts chose the random way in which questions
of international law are disposed of. In Xavier v. Canara Bank Ltd  (1969), the Kerala High Court
held that individual citizen could not complain about the breach of the International Covenants on
Human Rights in the municipal courts “ even if the country concerned has adopted the covenants
and ratified the Optional Protocol ”. At the time when this judgment was given, India was a party

7
to International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) and International Covenant on
Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR) which shows that the Court did not even evaluate
the difference between signing and ratification of treaties. In Biswambhar Singh v. Orissa  (1957),
the Orissa High Court observed that India is “ one of the parties to the Universal Declaration of
Human Rights ” which was a General Assembly resolution and does not require signature or
ratification process of a treaty.
24. April 2014 issue of ‘ UNCTAD IIA Issues Note’ indicated that by end of 2013, 98 States
have been respondents in a total of 568 known treaty-based cases which is indicative of the rising
trend of arbitration cases brought by States and international investors. The said report has also
indicated India as the eighth most frequent respondent State in 2013 with Czech Republic topping
the list.
F. India’s Role in International Law Making
25. The Ministry of External Affairs has informed the Committee that in recent years, the
approximate number of multilateral and bilateral treaties, agreements and memoranda of
understanding concluded annually is over three hundred on various subjects pertaining to different
administrative Ministries. All treaties and agreements that are in force and having the intention of
the States Parties to create legal obligations are binding and such treaties and agreements shall be
observed in good faith (pacta sunt servanda) . Approximately, around 3,500 treaties have been
concluded by India since 1950.
26. India is also a member of various international Dispute Settlement Bodies whose
responsibility is to determine disputes involved on the subject of the treaties. The presence of
competent experts on international law to represent in these bodies is bound to ensure the national
interest. It has, however, been observed that the Indian representations in some of the Dispute
Settlement Bodies has been minimal.

rounds of negotiations as under– –
“…it is a very asymmetrical mechanism. But, it is a sad reality that our negotiating teams
are not only small but they are stretched. I will give you an example. India is engaging with
Australia through the mechanism of RCEP . India also engages with Australia through the
WTO channels. India is also having a bilateral discussion which is going on a bilateral
relationship. On the Australian side, normally, for all these, they have three separate teams.
There may be some commonality. On our side, practically, it is the same set of negotiators
who have to handle all this.  While at one level, we have the advantage of having common
knowledge of what is happening on all three strands, but at the other level, our ability to
match their human manpower is stretched on our side. So, coming to the basic issue, in
fact, we would be very happy to strengthen our negotiating teams. We would be happy to
see an amalgamation of Ministry of Law as well as MEA handling the legal text . So,
additional manpower and additional legal help from both the Ministries would be of very
great use from our perspective. It is just a matter of making sure that the coordination and
the response becomes faster and not slower.  That is our basic concern in this issue. ”
36. During its interaction with the representatives of the Department of Agriculture, Co-
operation and Farmers’ Welfare, the Committee observed a disturbing variance between domestic
laws and international legal obligations due to overlap in the jurisdiction of Ministries. The witnesses
informed that the major international treaty recently entered by the Ministry is the International
Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture, which essentially involves a sub-set
from the Convention on Bio-diversity signed in 1982. That Treaty has an interface with the national
legislations, such as, the Bio-diversity Act, 2002 as well as Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) for
Plants, viz. the Protection of Plant V arieties and Farmers’ Rights Act, 2001 which is, in essence
handled by the Ministry of Environment and Forests.
36.1 To the query relating to cases of Indian women abandoned and destitute in foreign
countries, the representative of Ministry of Women and Child Development informed the Committee
that many such complaints have been received but the Ministry does not have any wherewithal and

16
therefore can only request the Ministry of Overseas Indian Affairs to intervene. Members are of the

present set-up of negotiations for international obligations is and our performance on earlier

mechanism in place right from the beginning of participation as player in the international fora,

3,000 investment agreements globally and out of which, over 600 cases have gone into arbitration.

redressal that investors get has been incorporated, as also to introduce that they have to approach

43.1 Members opined that cases in our system of dispute resolution in the conventional court
system could not be taken up as quickly as the international investors expect. Therefore, they
demand that arbitration should be made an alternative source of dispute resolution. In cases of
international arbitration, other international seats of arbitration have been opted to take up their
cases.  A situation then arises where our mechanism is not working in our own territory for the
purpose of that service of arbitration. A matured judicial system exists and our people are well-

voiced his apprehension of who represents the interests of the Ministry in the international

45.1  Another Member rejoined that out of the 189 UN Conventions on Labour only 45 including

the Government to not ratify these Conventions or whether they are just lying closed in office
records. The witness informed that the consent and agreement of various Ministries and agencies
where these laws are to be considered need to be obtained for which the Ministry is in the process
of consultations with them. The Committee observes that the treaty making process in vogue is
unarranged and better policy coordination on treaties and more accountability is required.
46. Chairman of UN International Law Commission deposed before the Committee and
highlighted a glaring instance of shortcoming in the procedure being currently followed. In his
words – –
“...there is a process of inter-Ministerial consultation even before the treaty negotiations are

charge of the topic, themselves have no clue as to what they want. We have faced this
problem in the Legal and Treaties Division on many occasions. For example, there were
negotiations to be held in the FAO. It was practically at the last minute that L&T Division
was informed and asked to prepare some notes. When we consulted the concerned Ministry,
they very generously told us, ‘We will do whatever you want. We will agree to whatever you
tell us’. We said that is not the issue. The issue is,where do your interests lie; what is the
country’ s interest and they have no clue on that.  So this is one problem which we face in
a number of areas where the Ministries which are in-charge of a particular topic, don’t
know what they are looking for. Then the Ministry of External Affairs has to come up with
ideas, try to guess as to where our interests lie ”.
