46.1. Speaking on the need for preparedness of meeting the obligations arising out of international
treaties and conventions, he stated that most of the treaties which India concludes, whether they
are bilateral or multilateral, don’t require implementing legislation. As soon as a treaty is ratified, the
country becomes a party and certain obligations arise.  One must be in a position to prosecute and
punish offenders and extend international cooperation to other countries who seek the extradition or
mutual legal assistance in respect of any offences. However, the experience has been that
legislations are slow in coming. He cited several instances such as the case of UN Transnational
Organised Crime, the UN Convention against Corruption, etc. where India went ahead with
ratification of the treaties in May, 2011 without having a law, but the required legislations are still
not made.
46.2. As regards the creation of a Department of International Law, he opined that placing the
Department within the Ministry of Law would forge complications relating to hierarchy and the
Law Secretary can always overrule the Department which would be detrimental to its effective
functioning. Therefore, the Department of International Law should be independent of the Ministry
of Law. He further argued that the source and process of formation of domestic law and
international law are very different which substantiate the need of their independence.
Recommendations/Observations of the Committee
47. The Committee observes that it has been the experience at international fora or at
the occasion of negotiating bilateral or multilateral treaties, the developed countries are
seen to be represented by large number of legal experts whereas Indian delegation is not
supported by matching number of legal experts. The Committee feels that our delegations
are not adequately equipped to that extent. The Committee wishes that at such occasions,
we should have equally capable negotiating team full of experts in domain and legal
knowledge with a view to instantly interpret provisions of negotiations and providing
alternative formula, if required, in the interest of the country.
48. The Committee observes that there is a need for creating a pool of experts in
various fields of the International Law to be drawn to different Departments/Organisations/
Institutions of the Government of India and the States in the capacity of legal advisors/
consultants, negotiators, experts in reporting in international fora and the multilateral and
bilateral talks. The Committee feels that such an institutional capacity will address the
immediate need of experts in the category of advisors, consultants, negotiators, drafting
experts in reporting in international fora and the multilateral/bilateral talks.
49. It feels that it is the need of the hour to streamline the existing mechanism of
handling all issues relating international co-operation and international legal obligations and
accordingly, recommends that the ‘Department of International Law’ may be created to
work as a nodal body to create a group of legal experts who will be serving the different
Ministries as and when it is required. This Department would be responsible to coordinate
and evolve specialised approach while negotiating any international convention or bilateral
or multilateral treaty. This process eventually would lead to involvement of legal experts as
well as domain experts from concerned Ministries at the fore-front of the negotiation

21
process and also accompanied by the officers of the Ministry of Law and Justice to advise on
the position of domestic law. The Department of International Law would have dual role i.e.,
ensuring the effective negotiations of treaties and its actual implementations at national
and international level. Finally, that Department would be able to develop a mechanism
providing for a more coherent, holistic and specialised approach among the state
institutions.
50. The Committee hopes that the newly created Department of International Law may
simultaneously develop the desired human resource, competent in matters relating to
international law, who may help the negotiators to develop a consistent approach on
international matters in international fora.
51. The Committee further observes that Department of International Law would be
repository of all the binding international Conventions, Bilateral/Multilateral treaties,
Resolutions and rules relating thereto.  The Department should also publish the same. This
would sensitise about the issues/subject involved to the country’s institutions and also the
people at large. The Department of International Law would further be mandated to bring
to the notice of all courts/tribunals in the country about the new interpretations given by
International Court(s) or Tribunals on any subject.
52. The Committee feels that it is now well settled that international law is no longer
limited to the regulation of diplomatic relations between States.  The gap between the
international courts and the domestic courts has now been substantially narrowed.  It,
therefore, calls for the incorporation of international norms into the national law as the
international law/rules/norms today aim at the matters which were earlier exclusively
belonged to the domestic jurisdiction of States and conversely, the domestic courts also deal
with the issues relating to international law.  The Committee accordingly feels that setting
up of this Department would be a step in filling up of the gap between the two.
53. Hence, the Committee recommends for setting up of a new Department of
International Law similar to the existing Department of Legal Affairs, Legislative
Department and Department of Justice.  The Ministry can be renamed as Ministry of
International Law, Domestic Law and Justice.
54. The Committee notes that as per existing practice, the Ministries/Departments have
the responsibility to implement India’s obligations in respect of the subjects pertaining to
them as per Government of India (Allocation of the Business) Rules, 1961. The Committee,
however, feels that it would certainly be in fitness of things that there is a need for creation
of a new ‘Department of International Obligations & Implementations’ under the direct
supervision of Prime Minister in the line of Department of Space, etc. The Committee feels
such a Department will provide for a monitoring mechanism at apex level and will further
strengthen the existing system. This would enhance the status of India in the community of
Nations as India aspires to be a Member of United Nations Security Council and also claims
to be an Economic Power.
55. It is further recommended that these two new Departments should be headed by
international law professionals and experts for a fixed term in the rank of Secretary aided

22
by Joint Secretary level officers from Indian Foreign Service, Indian Administrative Service,
other Central services and if needed, by the experts in the relevant fields who will co-
ordinate with various Departments and Ministry of External Affairs and Embassies/High
commissions.
56. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of External Affairs,  Ministry of Law
and Justice (to be rechristened as Ministry of International Law, Domestic Law and Justice)
and the concerned nodal Ministry designated for such negotiations should work as ‘Trinity’
in all negotiations of any bilateral/multilateral Treaties/International Conventions etc. The
Department of International Obligation & Implementation which may be under the direct
supervision of Prime Minister’s Office (PMO), as suggested above, is to work as overall
overseeing the working of the Trinity towards the implementation of  post-Treaty
obligations.
57. Through this Report, the Committee seeks to bring about structural changes and
capacity building in the present Ministry of Law and Justice by creating one more
Department in this Ministry, namely, Department of International Law as a part of legal
and judicial reforms. The Committee accordingly proposes that the Ministry should be
rechristened as Ministry of International Law, Domestic Law and Justice. The Committee
also suggests the following roadmap for strengthening the present Departments of Ministry
of Law and Justice:
(A) Department of Legal Affair: The appointment of Law Officers from the
Attorney General down to Prosecutors, and Government Advocates, Notary
Public should be looked through the prism of International Law for their
knowledge on International Law and practice. Some specialised Lawyers/legal
advisors are to be infused at various level in addition to refreshing the
existing nominees and appointees to get International Law exposure and
application in their day to day working. The Indian Law Institute (deemed
University) should have special courses in international law focussing on the
contemporary international law.  It is also suggested that Indian Society of
International Law (ISIL) Academy may be evolved into “Centre of Excellence”
in the field of International Law, as a pioneer institute in this field, if
necessary, through a Parliamentary enactment. The Committee wishes that
ISIL may be mandated for developing the human resources in the field of
ever growing Contemporary International law– –  by making, drafting,
interpreting, implementing and enforcing through sovereign State and the
three pillars of the Constitution of India, viz., the Parliament, the Executive
and the Judiciary.
(B) Legislative Department: The Legislative Department may strengthen the
existing Institute of Constitutional and Parliamentary studies (ICPS) by
shifting to allotted land in Chanakyapuri and remodel its syllabus and
curriculum of Legislative drafting in International Law and Domestic and
State Laws.

23
(C) Department of Justice: The Judiciary from Supreme Court down to the level
of Subordinate judiciary, Quasi Judicial Tribunals and adjudicative mechanism
are to be equipped with International Laws through National Judicial Academy
and State Judicial Academies. Sufficient financial support should be provided
by Union Government.

He then requested the Departments to highlight their roles in the process of drafting and negotiation
of international treaties. He stressed on the need of training the law officers of the Government in
the nuances of international laws and also for the creation of another Department of International
Law which would function in tandem with the Ministry of Law and Justice and Ministry of

3. The Secretary, Department of Legal Affairs highlighted the current process of treaty making
in the country which primarily involves the administrative Ministry. He stated that the Ministry of
Law and Justice is also consulted in the process and based on the recommendations of other
stakeholders, India’s position regarding a treaty is finalized. He submitted that according to a ruling
of the Hon’ble Supreme Court, whenever there is a conflict between a domestic law and
international conventions, the domestic law prevails. In circumstances where a domestic law does
not exist, international laws are given due respect. He further submitted that when a situation arises
when the country flouts international laws, the country could always approach the international
bodies for a review of the treaty obligations. He stated that in case a country, before signing a
treaty, feels that it would not be able to implement some provisions of the treaty, the provisions of
the Vienna Convention allow the country to specify its reservations before acceding to it. He
supported the idea of creation of a separate Department which would have officers well versed
with international laws as well as domestic laws. This would reduce conflicts between national and
international  laws. He however, expressed reservations on the creation of an overarching

44
Department of International Laws as it would disturb the Allocation of Business Rules of the
Government of India. Further, he stated that it would be too cumbersome for one Department to
look after the implementation of the myriad of treaties.
4. The Director, Indian Law Institute gave an overview of the functioning of the Institute . On
the issue of conflict between domestic laws and international laws, he submitted that once a
country signs an international treaty, it is bound to adhere to its provisions and violation of treaty
by domestic legislation cannot be justified. However, he stated that some treaties like the
International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights have some provisions which allow parties to
create reservations on implementation of some provisions of the treaty in accordance with their
domestic legislative framework.
5. The Secretary, Department of Justice stated that the Department administers only three
MoUs mainly concerned with exchange of judges. She stated that even these are not being
implemented adequately. She stated that the Department consults and follows the advice of the
Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) on international treaties. The Joint Secretary, Department of
Justice stated that the primary responsibility in international treaty negotiations rest with the
administrative Ministry. He stated that although the Ministry of Law and Justice assists the officials
of the administrative Ministries, their exposure to international laws is limited. He suggested that
more support needs to come from both the Ministry of Law and Justice and the Legal & Treaties
(L&T) Division of MEA.
6. The Secretary, Legislative Department stated that the Department has no role to play in the
preparation and finalization of international treaties. He stated that the Department comes into
picture only once the draft legislation for implementation of treaties comes to the Department for
vetting.
7. The Director, National Judicial Academy suggested the need to create a central repository of
international treaties so that they can become easily accessible. This, according to her, would help
in spreading awareness about the international legal obligations. She also suggested that curriculum
in colleges need to be changed in order to incorporate contemporary issues in the curriculum. She
also suggested that a course for judges also needs to be started to make them aware of

REPORT
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the action taken by the Ministry of Law and
Justice on the recommendations/observations of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee
on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice in its Seventy-fifth Report on the Demands for Grants
(2015-16) of the Ministry. The Report was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on
the 28th April, 2015.
2. The Action Taken Replies have been received from the Department of Justice and Legislative
Department, Ministry of Law and Justice in respect of the recommendations contained in the above mentioned
Report, vide, their communication dated 27
th July and 16th September, 2015 respectively. The Action Taken
Replies of Department of Legal Affairs have not yet been received. Replies of Legislative Department and
Department of Justice have been categorised as follows:
Chapter – I : The recommendations/observations which have been accepted by the Ministry i.e., in
respect of paras 3.6, 3.9, 6.12, 6.28, 6.29, 6.42, 6.61, 6.6 and 6.62  of the Report. The Committee is
pleased to note that the Ministry has accepted these recommendations.
Chapter – II : The recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue
in view of the replies given by the Ministry i.e., in respect of paras 3.11, 3.16, 6.20, 6.23, 6.52, 6.58 and 6.9
of the Report. The Committee is convinced with the explanations advanced by the Ministry and does not
wish to pursue them as of now.
Chapter – III : The recommendations/observations in respect of which Committee has not accepted
replies given by the Ministry i.e., with regard to paras 6.33, 6.40, 6.48 and 6.55 of the Report. The Committee
expresses its concern for not accepting the recommendations of the Committee dealt with in Chapter – III
of this Report and desires that the Ministry should furnish logical explanation in respect of these
recommendations.
Chapter – IV  :  The recommendations/observations on which final replies of the Ministry of Law
and Justice have not been received. The Committee desires that Ministry should furnish action taken notes
in respect of recommendations categorised in Chapter – IV .
3. The recommendations/observations of the Committee in its Seventy-fifth Report, the ATRs furnished
by the Ministry and the Committee’s further recommendations/observations have been dealt with in the
succeeding Chapters.

Systematic V oters Education and Electoral Participation (SVEEP)
Recommendation/observation  of  the  Committee

this programme will help in reaching out to maximum number of voters, especially the youth and the

so that programme does not suffer because of lack of funds. [Para 3.6]
1.1. The Committee appreciates the activities of IIIDEM in promoting democracy by training election
officials, both domestic and international, which helps promote India’s soft power in countries of Asia and
Africa. The Committee feels that the amount allocated to IIIDEM may be reviewed at RE stage, so that a
permanent campus/building for the Institute may get constructed quickly for effective performance of its
activities. [Para 3.9]
Reply/ ATR of the Commission:
1.2. The Commission is grateful to the Parliamentary Standing Committee for their appreciation of the
activities under SVEEP and IIIDEM. In this connection, it is stated that the demand for additional funds
under the relevant sub-heads for the purpose will be sent to the Ministry of Finance at the time of submission

Committee’s further observation

when the proposal in this regard is received from National Judicial Academy, Bhopal.

2.2. The  Committee  notes  the  reply.
Recommendation  of  the  Committee
3. The Committee notes that for the year 2015-16, an allocation ` 562.99 crore has been made
towards CSS for development of subordinate courts against the allocation of ` 1095 crore for the year
2014-15. The Committee also notes from the written reply to the questionnaire by the Department that
allocation for this year has been made keeping in view the revision of funding pattern of central assistance
under CSS from 75:25 to 50:50 in view of the higher devolution to states. The Committee feels that the
scheme has to a great extent helped in the development of infrastructure in subordinate courts. The
Committee hopes that in the proposed revised pattern, the states would continue to have adequate financial
resources to implement the scheme. The uneven allocation to different states over the last few financial
years is a matter of concern and Committee would like Department to look into the causes of wide
fluctuation in funds sanctioned to States in different years with a view to make consistent allocations to
the States.  [Para 6.28]
Action T aken  by  the  Ministry/Department
3.1. The primary responsibility of infrastructure development for the subordinate judiciary rests with the
State Governments. The Central Government augments the resources of the State Governments by releasing
financial assistance under a centrally sponsored scheme for the development of judicial infrastructure. The
scheme has been in place since 1993-94, and was revised in 2011. It covers the construction of court
buildings and residential accommodation of judicial officers of district and subordinate courts. As of March,
2015, the Central Government had released an amount of ` 3,131 crore to the State Governments and UT
Administrations under the revised funding pattern from 2011-12 to 2014-15. This represents a significant
increase over the sum of ` 1,245 crore that was provided by the Central Government in the initial phase of
the scheme from 1993-94 to 2010-11. During the last financial year (2014-15), an amount of ` 933 crore
was released to the States.
3.2. Funds under the centrally sponsored scheme for development of infrastructural facilities for
judiciary are released to the States after obtaining the utilization certificates for the grants released in the
previous years as per the guidelines of the scheme. While examining the proposals received from the State
Governments, the projections made at the time of the revision of the scheme in 2011 for requirement of
funds for judicial infrastructure in the State for a time span of five years are also kept in view. The overall
release of funds during the financial year, however depends on the budgetary allocations made for the
scheme.
3.3. The Joint Conference of Chief Ministers of States and Chief Justices of High Courts was
convened on 5
th April, 2015 to discuss the broad agenda of judicial reforms. With the enhanced
devolution of funds to the States on the recommendations of the 14 th Finance Commission it now
falls on the State Governments to increase investment in justice sector. It was accordingly resolved
that Chief Justices and Chief Ministers shall institute a mechanism for regular communication among
themselves to resolve issues particularly those relating to infrastructure and manpower needs and
facilities for the judiciary.

of the judiciary and help in quicker delivery of justice and reduction of arrears. The Committee hopes the
States would take full benefit of the scheme to upgrade and modernise the infrastructure in the subordinate
courts of the State. [Para 6.29]

halls / court rooms available for district and subordinate courts. In addition to these, 1003 court rooms were

as on 31
st December, 2014 reported by these High Courts, it may be seen that adequate infrastructure is
available for the current judicial manpower. Further, there are about 2,251 additional court rooms under
construction in States and UTs to take care of immediate increase in the working strength of judges in

and litigants. The Committee recommends that the High Courts of Gujarat, Delhi and Madhya Pradesh be

5.1. NJDG data will also help the judiciary in judicial monitoring and management and the Government to

5.2. The  Committee  notes  the  reply.

6. Article 348 provides for the use of Scheduled languages, other than English, with the consent of the

1. The Committee appreciates the initiatives of Commission to introduce VVPAT and feels that the
introduction of VVPAT in elections will go a long way in resolving the doubts created in the mind of the

Recommendation/observation  of  the  Committee
2. The Committee appreciates the work of Election Commission of India in creating a Web Portal of 84
crores of registered voters which has been launched on 25
th January, 2015. Such an attempt would reduce
multiple entries of electors at different places and resultant chances of bogus voting. All the voters have been
requested by the Election Commission of India to delete their multiple entries for the sake of authenticity of
8

9
the voter list. The Committee notes that the Election Commission of India has launched this programme for
purification and authentification of voters list on 3 rd March, 2015 for the sake of free and fair election. As
defective Electoral roll vitiates the election process and the results, there is need for maintaining accurate
and authentic voters list. The Committee feels that the onus lies equally on Election Commission of India,
State Election Commissions, Political parties as well as voters. The Committee is of the view that, the
State Election Commissions should in co-ordination with the ECI update the voter database already available
online. It would be proper if the same electoral roll is used for elections to PRIs and Municipalities. The
Committee accordingly impresses upon the Election Commission of India and the State Election
Commissions to conduct various elections from local bodies to Parliament on the basis of a common
electoral roll. [Para 3.16]
Action T aken  by  the  Ministry/Department
2.1. The electoral rolls for the Assembly and Parliamentary Constituencies are prepared under the provisions
of Sections 15 and 13D of the Representation of the People Act, 1950. The Provisions of the Representation
of the People Act, 1950 and the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, made there under are applicable with
respect to all matters relating to the preparation of electoral rolls for assembly/parliamentary constituencies.
2.2. The responsibility of preparation of electoral rolls of panchayats/municipalities elections rests with
the State Election Commission of the State concerned under Articles 243K and 243ZA of the Constitution of
India. In the current system, the Election Commission prepares electoral rolls for Parliamentary and Assembly
constituencies, and the State Election Commissions prepare electoral rolls for local bodies’ elections. However,
preparation of common electoral rolls involves the following issues:
(i) The States/UTs have their own separate state laws and amendment/modification in the same
will also be required to adopt the electoral rolls of the Election Commission of India, for
creation of common electoral roll. (While some States have coordinated their electoral rolls
with those prepared by the Election Commission, there are still some States that significantly
modify them). Some States even have different qualifying dates for the rolls got prepared by
SECs and those got prepared by the Election Commission of India.
(ii) There is no uniform system for preparation of rolls by SEC in all States.
(iii) Present database control tables pertaining to the ECI have the particulars of administrative

Action Taken  by  the  Ministry/Department
6.1. The problem of shortage of judges is being addressed through a two pronged strategy. Firstly, by
filling up the large number of existing vacancies in the judiciary and secondly, increasing the sanctioned
strength of judges. It would be pertinent to note that as per the Constitutional framework the selection and
appointment of judges in subordinate courts is the responsibility of State Governments and High Courts. On
account of the concerted efforts made by all stakeholders there has been a gradual increase in the sanctioned
strength of the subordinate judiciary over the past few years. It has increased from 17,715 at the end of
2012 to 20,214 in December, 2014.
6.2. In case of the High Courts, the Chief Justice of India gave an ‘in principle’ concurrence in April,
2014 to the joint recommendation of the Chief Ministers and Chief Justices Conference to increase the
sanctioned strength of High Courts by 25 per cent. Several States have already accepted this proposal, as a
result of which the sanctioned strength of High Courts has increased to 1017 judges as of June, 2015, as
against 906 in March, 2014. The judge-population ratio in the country, taking into account judges at all levels
now stands at about 17 judges per one million of the population.
6.3. However , it is noted that despite the gradual increase in sanctioned strength, there still remain
a large number of vacancies in subordinate courts. As of 31st December, 2014, there were 4,580
vacancies in the posts of judicial officers, representing about 22.66 per cent of the sanctioned strength.
Recently, in the Conference of Chief Justices held on 3rd and 4th April, 2015 it was resolved that the
Chief Justices of the respective High Courts shall take effective and speedy steps to fill up the
existing vacancies.
6.4. Department of Justice had submitted a comprehensive proposal to the 14th Finance Commission
which inter-alia  provided for setting up of additional courts in districts with high pendency of cases, re-
designing existing court complexes to make them more litigant friendly, enhancing access to justice and
capacity building of judicial manpower. Commission noted that proposal amounting to ` 9,749 crore has
been arrived at after an extensive consultation process with the State Governments. The Finance
Commission has endorsed the proposal and urged the State Governments to use the additional fiscal
space provided by them in the tax devolution to meet the requirement of additional infrastructure and
manpower for judiciary. 
6.5. As a result of concerted efforts made by various stakeholders the increasing trend of pendency of
cases in subordinate courts has been checked and the overall pendency in subordinate courts has declined
from 2.77 crore in 2010 to 2.64 crore in 2014.

Recommendations  of  the  Committee
1. The Committee appreciates the initiative of National Mission for Justice Delivery and Legal Reforms.
The Committee however notes that only a token amount of ` 1 lakh has been made for it in BE (2015-16)
which implies that Ministry is still in the process of finalizing details of the Mission. The Committee finds it
rather shocking that a Mission started in 2011 with a time frame of five years has still not taken off. The
Committee desires the Ministry to ensure that the Mission is taken seriously and implemented in a time
bound manner and objectives of the Mission are achieved. [Para 6.33]
Action T aken  by  the  Ministry/Department
1.1. National Mission for Justice Delivery and Legal Reforms was set up in August, 2011 with the twin
objectives of increasing access by reducing delays and arrears in the system and enhancing accountability
through structural changes and by setting performance standards and capacities. The Mission has been
pursuing a co ordinated approach for phased liquidation of arrears and pendency in judicial administration,
which, inter-alia, involves better infrastructure for courts including computerisation, increase in strength
of subordinate judiciary, policy and legislative measures in the areas prone to excessive litigation, re-engineering
of court procedure for quick disposal of cases and emphasis on human resource development. 
1.2. The Mission has taken several steps in each of the strategic areas towards fulfilment of its objectives.
All States have formulated their Litigation Policies with a view to reduce the Governmental litigation. State
Governments have been requested to make an assessment of the impact of the State Litigation Policies on
controlling proliferation of litigation by State agencies. Department of Legal Affairs have formulated National
Litigation Policy, 2015, which is under active consideration of the Government.
 1.3. An Inter-Ministerial Group (IMG) was constituted to suggest necessary amendments to the Negotiable
Instruments (NI) Act along with other policy and administrative measures to check increasing litigation
relating to cheque bounce cases. The IMG has suggested a number of measures including procedural and
legislative changes to reduce number of cheque bounce cases. Policy and legislative changes have also been
recommended to tackle the large number of cases that are arising under the provisions of Motor Vehicles
Act, 1988 (MV Act). A Plan Scheme for Action Research and Studies on Judicial Reforms is being implemented
to inter-alia promote action research on judicial reforms. Five projects of Action Research have been sanctioned
so far under the scheme.
1.4. An important aspect of the judicial reforms relates to re-engineering court procedures and court
processes for early disposal of cases. Process service has been identified as a major bottleneck for timely
14

15
delivery of justice. A research note was prepared and circulated to High Courts for improving the process
service in civil and criminal matters. A positive response has been received from several High Courts on the
suggestions made in the research note. The subject matter of re-engineering of court process and case
management is also under active consideration of the National Court Management System (NCMS) of the
Supreme Court. Process re-engineering exercise is being carried out under e-Courts Mission Mode Project.
For promotion of alternative methods of dispute resolution, mediation centres are being set up in court
complexes at District and Taluka levels. Government agencies are being encouraged to include arbitration /
mediation clauses in government contracts.
1.5. Shortage of judicial officers / judges in district and subordinate courts is one of the main causes
for backlog and pendency of cases in courts. The National Mission has regularly pursued this matter with
the State Governments and the High Courts. As a result of the concerted efforts of all the stakeholders,
the sanctioned strength of judicial officers / judges in district and subordinate courts has increased from
17,715 at the end of 2012 to 20,214 in December, 2014. The mission is pursuing the matter with the High
Courts for filling up the existing vacancies. Emphasis is also being laid on proper training of all court
functionaries.
1.6. The primary responsibility of infrastructure development for the subordinate judiciary rests with the
State Governments. The Central Government augments the resources of the State Governments by releasing
financial assistance under a Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) for development of judicial infrastructure.
Until 2011, the Central and State Governments used to contribute an equal share under the scheme but from
2011-12 onwards the fund-sharing pattern has been revised with the Central Government contributing 75%
of the funds. In case of States in the North-Eastern region, the Central Government provides 90% of the
funding. Central funding is, however, subject to budgetary allocation for the Scheme. As of March, 2015,
the Central Government has released an amount of `3131 crore to the State Governments and UT
administrations under the revised funding pattern from 2011-12 to 2014-15. This represents a significant
increase over the sum of `1,245 crore that was provided by the Central Government in the initial phase of
the scheme from 1993-94 to 2010-11.
1.7. Pendency reduction campaign was initiated for the first time in 2011. High Courts were requested to
prioritise disposal of cases that had been pending for a long duration, particularly those relating to senior
citizens and marginalised sections of society. In 2012 the focus of the campaign was to make the judicial
system free of cases that were over five years old. Pendency reduction campaign in 2013 focused on
weeding out ineffective and infructuous cases from the judicial system. In 2014 emphasis was laid on filling
up of vacancies of judicial officers and organization of Mega Lok Adalats. As a result of concerted efforts
made by various stakeholders the increasing trend of pendency of cases has been checked and the overall
pendency in subordinate courts has declined from 2.77 crore in 2010 to 2.64 crore in 2014. 
1.8. The establishment expenditure on National Mission is being met from the non-plan budget specifically
provided for the purpose. The budget head for National Mission Action Plan Implementation was created to
inter-alia undertake policy research activities to support the initiatives of National Mission. A technical
support cell was created for the National Mission under Access to Justice project being implemented in
partnership with UNDP. The budget for this purpose has been earmarked at `60.00 lakh under this project.
As such only a token provision of `1 lakh was made under the above budget head for the current financial
year. However the expenditure on e-Courts, construction of courts and residences for judges is also part of
the judicial reforms being undertaken by the Mission.

REPORT
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the action taken by the Ministry of Personnel,
Public Grievances and Pensions on the recommendations/observations of the Department-related Parliamentary
Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice in its 78
th Report on the Demands for
Grants (2015-16) of the Ministry. The Report was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok
Sabha on the 28th April, 2015.
2. The Action Taken Replies have been received from the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and
Pensions in respect of the recommendations contained in the above mentioned Report, vide,  their
communications dated 20th  May, 2015,  9th June, 2015 and 28th July, 2016. These replies have been categorised
as follows :
Chapter – I : The recommendations/observations which have been accepted by the Ministry i.e., in
respect of paras 1.2., 2.4., 3.3., 4.2., 5.2., 6.2., 7.2., 8.2., 9.2., 10.3., 11.2., 12.5., 13.2., 14.5.15.2.,16.2.,
17.2., 18.2., 19.2., 20.2., 21.4., 22.3., 23.7., 24.2., 25.3., 26.2., 28.3., 29.3., 30.6., 31.2. and 32.2.of the
Report. The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry has accepted these recommendations.
Chapter – II : The recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue
in view of the replies given by the Ministry i.e.,  in respect of paras 33.2., 34.3., 35.3., 36.2., 37.2., 38.3.,
39.5., 40.2., 41.2., 42.3., 43.2., and 44.3.  of the Report. The Committee is convinced with the explanations
advanced by the Ministry and does not wish to pursue them as of now.
Chapter – III : The recommendations/observations in respect of which Committee has not accepted
replies given by the Ministry i.e., with regard to paras 45.3., 46.2., of the Report. The Committee expresses
its concern for not accepting the recommendations of the Committee dealt with in Chapter – III of this
Report and desires that the Ministry should furnish logical explanation in respect of these recommendations.
Chapter – IV : The recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Ministry
have not been received i.e., with regard to paras 47.2., 48.2. and 49.2.of the Report, the Committee observes
that the Ministry has furnished evasive or interim replies in response to these recommendations. The Committee
desires that the Ministry should furnish action taken notes in respect of the recommendations dealt with in
Chapter – IV of this report.
3. The recommendations/observations of the Committee in its 76

Ministry and the Committee’s further recommendations/observations have been dealt with in the succeeding
Chapters.

and, if so required, funds may be made available at the RE (2015-16) stage so that important schemes of the
Department do not suffer for want of requisite funds. (Para 2.16)

ensuring optimum utilization of given allocation, to ensure that important schemes of the Department do not
suffer for want of funds.

Protection of Whistle Blowers
Recommendation/observation
39. The Committee expresses its strong displeasure over non implementation of the Lokpal and Lokayuktas
Act, 2013 and the Whistle Blowers’ Protection Act. It is unfortunate that the Ministry has so far not taken
any steps to amend the Whistle Blowers Protection Act though it maintains that amendments are needed
before the Act can be implemented. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should take necessary
action for quick opprationalisation of both the Acts. (Para 3.10)
Action Taken Reply
39.1 The Whistle Blowers Protection Bill, 2011 was passed by the Lok Sabha on the 27th of December,
2011 and was transmitted to the Rajya Sabha. Subsequently, it was noticed that some of the provisions in the
Bill needed a relook with a view to strengthening the safeguards against disclosures which may prejudicially
21

22
affect the sovereignty and integrity of the country, security of the State, etc. Accordingly, notices for certain
official amendments were given to Rajya Sabha Secretariat from time to time. The Bill was finally taken up
for consideration and passing on 21st February, 2014. However, as the Bill was taken up on the last day of
the last Session of the 15th Lok Sabha, the official amendments which had been given notice of, were not
moved during consideration and passing of the Bill on the said date. The Bill was passed by the Rajya Sabha
without any amendments ( i.e., in the same form as passed by the Lok Sabha) on 21st February, 2014. The
Bill has received the assent of the President on 9th May, 2014 and has become the Whistle Blowers Protection
Act, 2011 (No. 17 of 2014). In view of this, the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2011 requires some
amendments (aimed at safeguarding against disclosures affecting sovereignty and integrity of India, security
of the State, etc.), before it is brought into force. To make these amendments to the Act, the Government
has introduced the Whistle Blowers Protection (Amendment) Bill, 2015 in the Lok Sabha on 11th May, 2015
which has been passed by the Lok Sabha on 13
th May, 2015. Notices are proposed to be issued for consideration
and passing of the said Bill in the Rajya Sabha during the ensuing Monsoon Session. Thus, the Department
has already taken action for expeditious implementation and enforcement of the Whistle Blowers Protection
Act, 2011. The same will be brought in force after the Parliament passes the aforesaid amendment Bill and
Presidential assent thereto is received.
39.2 The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Bill, 2011, after being passed by both the Houses of the Parliament has
become an Act titled “The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 (1 of 2014)” which was brought into force
with effect from 16
th January, 2014 vide notification of the same date. The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act,
2013 requires some amendment so as to provide for situations where the composition of the Selection
Committee is deficient / incomplete due to absence of Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha, etc. Accordingly,
Lokpal & Lokayuktas and other related law (Amendment) Bill 2014 was introduced in Lok Sabha on 18.12.2014.
The same has been referred to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances,
Law& Justice and is presently under consideration of the Committee. The Parliamentary Standing Committee
considering the Lokpal and Lokayuktas and other related Law (Amendment) Bill, 2014 has so far held its
meetings on the Bill on 08-01-2015, 03-03-2015, 08-04-2015, 15-04-2015 and 26.05.2015. Further one
more meeting has been scheduled for 16.07.2015. Besides this, the Standing Committee has also undertaken
study-visit on the said Bill to Kolkata, Mumbai, Hyderabad, Tirupati and Chennai from 14th to 23rd June,
2015 and to Srinagar from 10th July to 12th July, 2015. Further action can only be taken by the Government
after the Standing Committee submits its report on the said Bill.
Committee’s further observation

no significant deficit in promotion quota in IAS. (Para 3.22)
Action Taken Reply
41.1 This Department has taken various steps to ensure that the State Civil Services Officers get their
induction into IAS in time. The process of determination of vacancies in all the States / Joint Cadres of IAS
was initiated well in advance and was completed by 31 st March, 2015 after having meetings with the State
Governments. In the Meeting with the Principal Secretary (GAD) of all the State Governments held on
18.05.2015 the State Governments were impressed upon to send their proposals to UPSC for convening of
Selection Committee Meetings for preparation of the Select List 2014 (SCS) and 2014 (Non-SCS) in respect
of all States/Cadres latest by October, 2015. Instructions have been issued to the State Governments to
publish the seniority list of their State Civil Services officers and also to standardize the mechanism of
submission of ACRs of these officers so as to enable it to prepare the Select Lists expeditiously. This
department also participates in the zonal review meetings conducted by UPSC so as to monitor the progress
of recruitment by promotion. Further the promotion regulations have been made more exact and transparent
so as to reduce the scope of litigation.
Committee’s further observation
41.2 The Committee takes note of the reply and hopes that the Department would take proactive
measures to ensure that there is no deficit in either of the cadres.

Recommendation/observation

24
quality of investigation of CBI. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should take all
possible steps to ensure prompt filling of vacancies in CBI. (Para 4.4)
Action Taken Reply
42.1 Occurrence and filling up 9fvacancies is a continuous process. The number of vacancies keeps on
varying depending on the induction, promotion, repatriation and retirement of officers. Department of
Personnel and Training concerned with filling up posts of level of SP and above in CBI has filled up a
number of vacant posts at senior level on the recommendations of CBI Selection Committee held frequently.
42.2 CBI, responsible with filling up vacancies at junior level executive posts, has made persistent efforts
to fill up these posts by various methods of recruitment. CBI as well as Department of Personnel & Training
has pursued with SSC to expedite process of selection for junior executive posts to be filled up by direct
recruitment. Similarly, CBI has pursued with UPSC to expedite vacant executive/legal/Technical posts in
CBI at different levels. CBI has also taken steps for conducting DPCs to expedite appointments for vacant
executive posts at various levels by promotion in time bound manner.
42.3 Various measures/steps have been taken to attract personnel to CBI in executive/technical posts at
various levels and to smoothen the process of recruitment by providing special dispensation/amendments in
the RRs of various posts as under :
Recruitment Rules in respect of various posts in CBI have been amended from time to time as
recommended by Parliamentary Standing Committee in its various reports in consultation with the
UPSC.
CBI has been exempted from consultation with UPSC for recruitment to the post of Dy. SP for a
period of three years.
There was 100% Direct Recruitment of constables in CBI which has been now dispensed with
keeping in view the expensive, long drawn and cumbersome exercise for a small organization like
CBI.
Efforts are being made to fill up vacant posts by promotion by relaxing the provisions of RRs as and
when sufficient numbers of eligible officers are not available in the feeder grade.
42.4 Attempts are being made to attract more officers to join CBI on deputation by modernizing CBI in
terms of equipments and machinery, infrastructural support, investigation tools, weaponry and vehicles,
designing special incentive allowances, increasing number of residential quarters, etc.

REPORT
CHAPTER - I
BRIEF OVERVIEW OF THE MINISTRY
1.0. The Union Ministry of Law and Justice comprises of three Departments, namely, the
Department of Legal Affairs, Legislative Department and Department of Justice and through the
said Departments, the Ministry assists in the process of orderly change directed towards realization
of the objectives set out in the Constitution.
DEPARTMENT OF LEGAL AFFAIRS
1.1. As per the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, the Department of
Legal Affairs renders advice to various Ministries/Departments of the Government of India on legal
matters and carry out the litigation work in various Courts, including the Supreme Court. Besides
this, it is also concerned with the appointment of Law Officers, namely the Attorney General for
India, the Solicitor General of India and the Additional Solicitor Generals of India, assists in
entering into treaties with foreign countries in matters of civil law on behalf of the President of
India. It is also the nodal authority in respect of Appellate Tribunal for Foreign Exchange, the
Income Tax Appellate Tribunal and National Tax Tribunal.
1.2. The Department of Legal Affairs has a two tier set up, namely, the Main Secretariat at New
Delhi and the Branch Secretariats at Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai and Bangalore. The nature of duties
discharged by the Main Secretariat and Branch Secretariats can be broadly classified into two areas
- Advice work and Litigation work. Advice caters to Central Government Departments/Offices at
Centre and in States/UTs and Litigation work relates to Central Administration Tribunal (CAT), High
Courts and Supreme Court.
1.3. The following are the organizations/institutions, which come under the overall supervision
of Department of Legal Affairs and get Grant-in-aid for their research works:-
(a) Law Commission of India: -  The Law Commission of India is a non-statutory
body, constituted by the Government once in three years. The Commission was first
constituted in 1955. It consists of a Chairman, three full-time Members, one
Member-Secretary and three or more part-time Members, depending upon the nature
of work. Law Commission Reports are considered to be primary source of law
reforms for Parliament, as well as the judiciary.
(b) Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT): -  Section 252 of the Income Tax Act,
1961 provides that the Central Government shall constitute an Appellate Tribunal
consisting of as many Judicial Members and Accountant Members as it thinks fit,
to exercise the powers and discharge the functions conferred on the Appellate
Tribunal by said Act.
(c) Appellate Tribunal of Foreign Exchange (ATFE): -  The Appellate Tribunal of
Foreign Exchange was established on 1
st June 2000 vide Government of India

2
Notification No. S.O. 531 (E), dated 1.6.2000 issued under section 18 of the
Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (FEMA),
(d) Indian Law Institute (ILI):- The Indian Law Institute registered under the
Societies Registration Act, 1860 is engaged in research in the field of law.
(e) International Centre for Alternate Dispute Resolution (ICADR):- The
International Centre for Alternate Dispute Resolution was registered under the
Societies Registration Act, 1860 on 31
st May 1995. It is an autonomous organisation
working under the aegis of the Department.
(f) Bar Council of India (BCI): - The Bar Council of India is a statutory body
constituted under the Advocates Act 1961, which has been empowered among other
things to lay down standards of professional conduct and etiquette for lawyers,
maintain and improve the standard of legal education in the country.
(g) Institute of Constitutional and Parliamentary Studies (ICPS):-  The Institute of
Constitutional and Parliamentary Studies is a private body engaged in research in the
field of constitutional and parliamentary studies and came into existence in 1965.
LEGISLATIVE DEPARTMENT
1.4. The Legislative Department acts mainly as a service provider in so far as the legislative
business of the Union Government is concerned. The Department is entrusted with legislative
matters and is responsible for drafting of all Government Bills and Ordinances and scrutiny and
vetting of subordinate legislations sponsored by various Union Ministries/ Departments. Rendering
assistance to Parliament and Joint/Standing Committees in respect to Bills before its enactment. It
is also administratively concerned with certain matters such as the Code of Civil Procedure,
Limitation and Arbitration, Contracts, Personal Laws, Evidence and Transfer of Property. There are
over hundred Central Acts falling under these subjects.
1.5. The Department has two wings under it mainly:-
(i) Institute of Legislative Drafting and Research : With a view to increase the
availability of trained legislative draftsmen in the country, the Institute of Legislative
Drafting and Research was established as a Wing of the Legislative Department,
Ministry of Law and Justice in January, 1989.
(ii) Official Languages Wing and Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan : The Official Languages
Wing is a successor Organisation of the Official Languages (Legislative) Commission
under the Legislative Department. It has been entrusted with the preparation and
publication of a standard legal terminology for use in all Official Languages;
authoritative texts in Hindi of all Central Acts and Ordinances and Regulations
promulgated by the President, all rules, regulations and orders made by the Central
Government under any Central Act and authoritative texts of all Central Acts and
Ordinances and Regulations promulgated by the President in the respective Official
Languages of the States and to arrange for the translation of all Acts passed and
Ordinances promulgated in any State into Hindi, if the texts of such Acts or
Ordinances are in a language other than Hindi.

3
1.6 Election Commission of India:  Legislative Department is also administratively concerned
with the Election Commission of India and Election laws connected with election to Parliament and
State Legislatures and to the offices of the President and the Vice-President. There is a separate
Demand No.55 for the Election Commission of India.
DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE
1.7. The duties of the Department of Justice, as per the Government of India (Allocation of
Business) Rules, 1961, include the administration of justice and the processing of appointment of
judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, appointment of Judicial Commissioners and Judicial
Officers in Union Territories, creation of All India Judicial Service and extension/exclusion of the
jurisdiction of a High Court to a Union Territory.
1.8. The following institutions/autonomous bodies/policy initiatives come directly under the
overall supervision of Department of Justice:
(a) Supreme Court of India:-  There is a separate demand No.57 (Appropriation)
pertaining to the Supreme Court of India. The expenditure to be incurred on the
Supreme Court of India is ‘Charged’
 expenditure .
(b) National Legal Services Authority (NALSA):-  The National Legal Services
Authority has been constituted under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 to
monitor and evaluate implementation of legal aid programmes and to lay down
policies and principles for making legal services available under the Act. The NALSA
issues guidelines for the State Legal Services Authorities to implement the legal aid
programmes which are in turn discharged through the following services:-
(i) Free Legal Services: It includes court fees, process fee and all charges
payable or incurred in connection with any legal proceedings, providing
Advocate in legal proceedings, etc.
(ii) Lok Adalats: -  Lok Adalat is a forum where the disputes/cases pending in
the court of law or at pre-litigation stage are settled/compromised amicably.
The Lok Adalat has been given statutory status under the Legal Services
Authorities Act, 1987.
(c) Family Courts/Special Courts :- The Family Court Act, 1984 was enacted with a
view to providing for establishment of Family Courts, to promote conciliation and
secure speedy settlement of disputes relating to marriage, family affairs and related
matters. In accordance with the provisions of section 3 of the Act, the State/UT
Governments can establish Family Courts in the areas comprising districts, towns,
city in the States having population of ten lakhs. Even the States/UTs are competent
to establish such court in those areas with the State/UT having a population less
than ten lakhs in consultation with the concerned High Court.
(d) National Judicial Academy :- The National Judicial Academy was registered as a
Society under the Societies Registration Act and came into existence with effect
from 17
th August, 1993. The affairs of the Academy are managed by a Governing

4
Council, which is chaired by the Chief Justice of India. The registered office of the
Academy is in Supreme Court Building at New Delhi and another office was
established in August, 2000 at Bhopal. The main objectives of the Academy are to
impart training to the Judicial Officers of the States/Union territories and to study
the court management and administration of justice in States and Union territories.
(e) Centrally Sponsored Scheme: The Government is implementing a Centrally
Sponsored Scheme (CSS) for development of infrastructure facilities for judiciary
since 1993-94. The scheme covers construction of court buildings and residential
accommodation of judicial officers/judges covering only Subordinate courts. Under
the Scheme, funds are provided to the States to augment their capacities for
infrastructure development of the District and Subordinate Courts. The modified
CSS is to be implemented in a Mission Mode approach over the years 2011-16 under
the National Mission.
(f) National Mission for Justice Delivery and Legal Reforms:  Set up for five years
in 2011, and became fully functional with effect from the financial year 2012-13.
The twin goals of the Mission include increasing access by reducing delays and
arrears in the system and enhancing accountability at all levels through structural
changes and setting performance standards and facilitating enhancement of
capacities for achieving such performance standards. The four schemes proposed to
be pursued under the Mission are as under;
(a) Scheme for Computerization of the District and Subordinate Courts / E-
Courts.
(b) Access to Justice - Government of India.
(c) Strengthening of Access to Justice in India (SAJI (EAP).
(d) Action Research and Studies on Judicial Reforms.
(g)   Access to Justice- Externally Aided Project (UNDP assisted)
The Project started in 2009 with support under the United Nations Development
Programme (UNDP). The Project is being implemented in 7 States (Bihar,
Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh) and
aims to strengthen access to justice for the marginalized - particularly women,
scheduled castes, scheduled tribes and minorities - by supporting strategies and
initiatives that seek to address the barriers they face.
 (h) Access to Justice- North-East and Jammu and Kashmir (Government of India
Project)
The Project started in 2012 and covers the 12
th Five year Plan period (2012-2017)
to venture in those regions of the Country which have so far been under-represented
and unheard in the arena and discourses of Access to Justice. The project aims to
make Justice accessible to the marginalised sections of the society. The project aims
to train lawyers, law students and customary judicial officers to raise awareness

5
among people about their legal rights. It is hoped that the project will be a milestone
in establishing a model of access to justice in remote areas of North East Region
and Jammu & Kashmir.
(i)    Computerization of District and Subordinate Courts E-courts Mission Mode
Project Phase-I & II :- This is a scheme proposed in the 12
th Plan with components
such as computerisation of 1000 new Courts, use of solar energy under e-Courts
Project, computerisation of the Public Prosecutors Office, videoconferencing facility
for jails, enhancement of ICT infrastructure of courts, digitization of old case
records, computerisation of Judicial libraries, up-gradation of application software,
SMS based services, Touch Screen Kiosks with a provision of ` 1280 crore which
would spread over a period of five years.
(j) Establishment of Gram Nyayalayas under the Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 :-
The Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 has been enacted by the Parliament to provide for
the establishment of the Gram Nyayalayas at the grass root level for the purpose of
providing speedy and inexpensive access to justice to the citizens at their door steps.
The Central Government would meet 50% of the recurring expenses to be incurred
on the setting up of these courts in the first three years subject to a ceiling of
` 3.20 lakhs per annum.
(k) The Fourteenth Finance Commission  has recommended ` 9,749 crore to the
Department of Justice for pendency reduction by establishing additional courts, Fast
Track Courts, establishment of Family Courts, redesigning existing courts to make
them litigant-friendly, augmenting technical support for e-courts, scanning and
digitalization, Access to justice- legal aid, Lok Adalats, ADR, Training and capacity
building of judges, public prosecutors, mediators and lawyers and establishing state
judicial academies for Manipur, Meghalaya and Tripura.

EVM & VOTER VERIFIABLE PAPER AUDIT TRAIL SYSTEM (VVPAT) 
3.12. V oter-verified paper audit trail (VVPAT) is a method of providing feedback to voters using
a ballot less voting system. Under VVPAT, a printer-like apparatus is linked to Electronic V oting
Machine (EVM). When a vote is cast, a receipt is generated showing the serial number, name and
symbol of the candidate. It confirms the vote and the voter can verify the details.
3.13. The Commission submitted that EVMs are produced by two public sector units, i.e. BEL
and ECIL. These are the only two units which are authorized to produce it and have the expertise
and all the securities relating to EVMs. So, EVMs and VVPATs are the two machines which are

15
to be procured in order to phase out the pre-2006 machines and to meet the demands for the Lok
Sabha elections. The Commission has informed that VVPAT was used in select polling stations in
8 States (Bihar, Karnataka, Chhattisgarh, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Uttar Pardesh and West Bengal) and
the Commission is overall satisfied with the VVPAT in these States. As against the demand for
` 1800 crores in BE (2016-17), an allocation of ` 1700 crores has been allocated for the purpose
to the Legislative Department, which is the administrative Department for the procurement of
EVMs and VVPATs.
3.14.  While making his submission before the Committee the Director-General, Election
Commission of India stated that the:-
….our total requirement of EVMs for 2019 General Elections is 16,35,000 VVP ATs,
16,35,000 Control Units and 22,37,000 Ballot Units. From the numbers available, the
balance which has to be procured is, 16,15,000 VVP ATs, 9,30,000 Control Units and
13,95,000 Ballot Units. So, these have to be procured before December, 2018 for the
elections to be conducted in 2019. Keeping the production capacity of the two companies,
i.e., BEL and ECIL, we have projected the requirement over the next three years, which
comes close to 
` 5,412 crores.
….for 2016-17, we have asked for ` 1,800 crores. So, every year, we will have to
do it because of the production capacity of these companies. If we give them only for one
year , they will not be able to produce it.
3.15. The Committee appreciates the Commission’s initiative for phasing out old EVMs and
plan to procure new EVMs and VVPATs from BEL and ECIL for the upcoming General
Elections to the Lok Sabha in 2019. The Committee is of the view that with the every general
election more and more voters’ turn out is expected, as recently noticed in the assembly
elections in the States of Assam and West Bengal. Since periodic elections are the epitome
of democracy, the Committee feels that fund allocated may be revised for the procurement
of EVMs and VVPATs during the RE stage so that the work of Commission does not suffer.
BOGUS VOTERS AND D VOTER (DOUBTFUL VOTER)
3.16.  The National Electoral Roll Purification and Authentication Programme (NERPAP), popularly
known as ‘India Roll Call’ has been launched on 3
rd March, 2015 with the objectives (i) to link
and authenticate the EPIC data of electors with Aadhaar data (ii) voluntary disclosure of the
electors concerned of the multiple entries pertaining to them and disposal of such cases within 15
days by the Electoral Registration Officer (iii) correct the errors of any elector if it is there in the
entry of the EPIC and (iv) improvement of the image quality of the EPIC.
3.17.  The Election Commission of India in its written submission on the Demands for Grants
(2016-17) submitted that:
...The Commission before every Summary Revision undertakes pre-revision activities.
During these activities, EROs run de-duplication software in their ACs and after field
verification on the basis of the findings of software through BLOs, multiple entries are
removed. The electors having multiple entries in electoral roll have been given option to

16
disclose the information voluntarily. During NERP AP , an initiative was also undertaken to
integrate Aadhar no. of electors with electoral database but in light of the Interim Order
of Hon’ble Supreme court in WP (Civil) No. 494 of 2012, the Commission suspended “all
further activities relating to collection/feeding/seeding of Aadhar number under NERP AP
with immediate effect till further directions”.
3.18. The names of those persons whose Indian citizenship was in question were to be referred
to the concerned Tribunals, for final decision of the Tribunals set-up under the Foreigners
(Tribunals) order, 1964. Meanwhile, those names were to be provisionally included in the electoral
rolls but the word ‘doubtful’ was to be indicated against such names in the relevant portion of the
electoral roll under the footnote “D” meaning doubtful/disputed. After the receipt of the final
decision from the concerned Tribunal, the Electoral Registration Officers (EROs) shall either delete
or allow remaining such names in the electoral rolls in accordance with the above cited said Court
order. During the pendency of their cases, “D” voters were not allowed to vote. As per the latest
figure furnished by CEO Assam  there are 136448 number of persons in the  Electoral Roll which
are the marked as ‘D’  Doubtful voter.
3.19. The Committee appreciates the work of Election Commission of India in checking
bogus voting by electoral role purification by linking it with Aadhar card. The Committee
feels that a common electoral roll will reduce cost, time and check electoral malpractices
in the country. The Committee, therefore, recommends that a common electoral be
prepared in the country which can be used from panchayat level to Parliamentary elections
with the State Election Commissions  to weed out multiple electoral rolls to check corrupt
practices during elections. The Committee also recommends the ECI to ensure that no
persons voting rights are hampered by wrongfully categorizing them as Doubtful voters as
it will go against the very principle of electoral democracy.
3.20. The Committee recommends to the ECI to consolidate all the guidelines into a
simplified ‘code’ and publish the same for the knowledge of all the stakeholders. It has
been observed that ‘Citizens’ and their family members are often harassed by stooping their
vehicle and their privacy is also eroded in the name of implementation of the electoral code
of conduct despite there being no evidence of any illegal activity. This calls for abundant
precaution on the part of implementing agencies.
3.21. As regards the resolution of disputes during elections, the Committee suggests that
cases registered during the period should be handled by Special Prosecutors and
Magistrates on a time bound manner.

A. NATIONAL MISSION FOR JUSTICE DELIVERY & LEGAL REFORMS
(SECRETARIAT EXPENDITURE)
6.5. The objective of the Mission is to increase access to justice by reducing delays and arrears
in the system and enhance accountability through structural changes and by setting performance
standards. The objectives were to be achieved in a time bound manner by the year 2015-16 through
a mission mode approach. The Mission has a Mission Directorate, an Advisory Council and a
Governing Council for overseeing the implementation of the Mission. The broad areas covered by
the National Mission are policy and legislative changes, re-engineering of procedures, human
resource development, leveraging Information and Communication Technology (ICT) and improve
physical infrastructure of subordinate courts.
6.6. In the BE (2016-17), a provision of ` 3.20 crore was made for non-plan Secretariat
expenditure under National Mission for Justice Delivery and Legal Reforms against ` 2.96 crores
in BE (2015-16) which was reduced at RE (2014-15) to ` 2.81 crore.

B. FAMILY COURTS
6.7 The Family Courts Act, 1984 provides for establishment of Family Courts by the State
Governments in consultation with the High Courts with a view to promote conciliation and secure
speedy settlement of disputes relating to marriage and family affairs and for matters connected
therewith. Under Section 3(1)(a) of the Family Courts Act, it is mandatory for the State
Governments to set up a Family Court for every area in the State comprising a city or a town
whose population exceeds one million. In other areas of the States, the Family Courts may be set
up if the State Governments deems it necessary. There are 438 functional family courts in the
country .
6.8 Central financial assistance started in the year 2002-03 with a non-recurring grant @ ` 10
lakh per court provided by the Department of Justice to the concerned States/UTs for setting up
of Family Courts and the concerned States to provide matching share. A further provision of ` 5 lakh
per court per annum for meeting running expenditure on Family Courts with matching share from
the concerned States was also put in place. In BE (2016-17) a provision of ` 0.01 crore has been
made for Family Courts/Special Courts. However, the Department of Justice in its written
submission to the Committee on the Demands for Grants (2016-17) submitted that Non-Plan grant
to Family Courts has been discontinued from 2016-17.
6.9 The Committee is unable to understand the reasons for discontinuation of Non-Plan
grants to the Family Courts when only 438 Family Courts have been established so far in
the country and most of these courts are still functioning in the conventional courts
complexes. The Committee instead feels that Family Courts not only needs to be
strengthened but separate complexes be set-up which should not be too far from the regular
courts.

6.10 The objectives of the Academy include the strengthening of the administration of justice
through judicial education, research and policy development. In the BE (2016-17) ` 20.74 crore has
been sought by the NJA and the same has been allocated to it. Out of 124 sanctioned posts, 36
are vacant in NJA.

for Grants (2016-17) apprised the Committee that

6.12 The Committee is happy to note that funds have been allocated for construction of
residential quarters for staffs. The Committee feels that vacant posts in NJA also need to
be filled-up to augment its human resource potential and more and more seminars and
training programmes on International Law needs to be organised for the judiciary so as to
equip them of the emerging legal scenario at global level.
6.13 NJA  is an autonomous statutory Institution being handled by Highest Judicial

34
officers and sitting Judges. The Committee desires that National Judicial Academy needs to
establish regional academies in East, South, West and Northern parts of the country to
strengthen the training requirements of judiciary at suitable locations, which may be other
than State capitals. The Committee also feels that NJA need to conduct seminar/conferences
at national level and international level, especially Asia-Pacific, Africa etc. so as to acquaint
judges in the country of the dynamics and innovations in the international legal system. The
Committee also recommends the Government to encourage the meeting of judges through
reciprocal programmes by bi-lateral and multi-lateral arrangements with all the countries
and Regional Groupings.
6.14 The Committee reiterates earlier recommendation contained in its Eightieth Report
on “Synergy between Tribal Justice System and Regular Justice System of the Country” to
have State Judicial Academies in every State especially in North Eastern States.

6.24 The Committee appreciates increased grants-in-aid to NALSA in the current financial
year. However, the Committee observes that NALSA’s allocation was revised to ````` 93.94
crores in RE (2015-16) from ````` 140 crore in BE (2015-16). The Committee is constraint to

allocated to it. The failure of NALSA to utilize the funds allocated is a serious problem and
the Committee is unable to understand the reasons for its non-utilization year after year.
The Committee recommends NALSA to proactively utilise funds allocated to it during each
financial year by undertaking new initiatives/schemes or revamping its existing schemes
especially legal aid services to the poor.
6.25 One of the thrust areas of NALSA includes delivery of legal aid to the poor and
marginalised sections of the society. However, the Committee during its deliberations with
various stakeholders during its study-visit to Nagpur Jail, Maharashtra observed that there
are serious lacunae in the legal aid delivery by the NALSA and State Legal Services
Authority (SLSA). The under trials were not given proper legal aid and the Committee
takes very serious note of it. The Committee accordingly, recommends NALSA to monitor
the activities of SLSAs in various States in the area of legal aid as non-delivery of proper
legal aid to the marginalised sections is contrary to the very objective for which NALSA was
established.
6.26 One of the activities of NALSA is to undertake and promote research in the field of
legal education. The Committee accordingly, recommends NALSA to undertake research in
legal aid and education with national law schools in the country to identify bottlenecks in
its programmes/schemes and also to promote legal aid education.
6.27 The court fee paid to panel lawyers is very low and is difficult for NALSA to attract
competent lawyers. Since NALSA has already constituted a Committee on the issue, the
Committee, feels that the fee of panel lawyers and defence lawyers should be raised
reasonably and revise it periodically so that quality legal aid services can be provided to the
poor litigants.
6.28 The Committee feels that the Government should be in a position to appoint defense
lawyer at par with Prosecutor and Assistant Prosecutor (cadre appointee) to work under the
National Legal Services Authority (NALSA). More so, the privacy of the accused in custody
should be maintained to give instruction and participate in legal consultation on bail, trial
and appeal matters by the visit of the NALSA lawyers. There should be a separate room
constructed by NALSA in every Jail for such consultation and the defense lawyers appointed
should have proper consultation with the prisoners before appearing on their behalf in
courts, as the present system of arguing cases without the instruction of clients and in the
absence of clients is against human rights and fundamental rights guaranteed by the
Constitution of India. The Committee is also of the view that NALSA should provide TA &

COMPUTERISATION OF DISTRICT AND SUBORDINATE COURTS
(i) e-Courts Mission Mode Project Phase-I
6.40 The e-Courts Integrated Mission Mode Project approved in the year 2010 is one of the
National e-Governance projects (NeGP), being implemented for ICT enablement of district and
subordinate Courts of the country and envisages computerisation of 14,249 District and
Subordinate courts by 31
st March, 2015.
6.41 The objective of the e-Courts project is to provide designated services to litigants, lawyers
and the judiciary. The project facilitates automation of case management workflow through use of
application software for activities such as Case Filing, Scrutiny, Registration, Case Allocation, Court
Proceedings, Details entry of a Case, Case Disposal & restoration, Transfer of Case, Pendency data
/Institution Registers, Court Diaries, Calculation of court fees etc. The national e-Courts portal
(http://www.ecourts.gov.in)  provides online services to litigants such as details of case registration,
cause list, case status, daily orders, and final judgments. Currently, litigants can access case status
information in respect of over 6.04 crore pending and decided cases and more than 2.41crore
orders/judgements pertaining to district and subordinate Courts.
6.43. The Department in its written submission stated that sites for all 14,249 courts (100%) have
been made ready for computerisation, out of which LAN has been installed at 13,643 courts
(95.75%), hardware at 13,436 courts (94.3%) and software at 13,672 courts (96%). The

45
Department also submitted that change management exercise has been completed in all the High
Courts and more than 18000 judicial officers and staffs have been trained in UBUNTU-Linux and

under the supervision of e-Committee of Supreme Court. Based on the experience of pilots, it was
decided in consultation with the e-Committee of Supreme Court of India to provide VC facilities
for 488 Court complexes and 342 jails out of which equipment has been delivered at 667 locations.
Apart from VC facilities being provided under the e-Courts Project, some States have already
implemented VC in courts from their own resources.
